A tool built on top of the engine could select and repair a full candidate against hard and soft constraints, for example with a MaxSMT solver over the variant space. MaxSMT (maximum satisfiability modulo theories) seeks a solution that satisfies all hard constraints while satisfying as many soft constraints as possible, or maximizing their total weight. Section 8 of Programming Z3 describes this form of optimization. That capability is not part of the current engine. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.

Figure 2: A pipeline for clustering candidate formalizations, locating recurring disagreements, and routing each disagreement to an appropriate check. Cluster sizes and review-item counts are from the user guide’s larger Dogwood study

Use a semantic-diff budget in continuous integration (CI). The command (checkau A B :max_size N :algorithm exact) prints nothing on success and causes the program to fail when the anti-unifier exceeds the budget. Every printed result in the user guide is pinned this way, so the guide and the engine can’t drift apart. The same command can serve as a regression gate. Set a maximum result size for a reference formalization and a regenerated one, and fail the pipeline when the anti-unifier exceeds it. The binary follows standard shell conventions: Results go to stdout, diagnostics (ok --- N nodes) go to stderr, and the process exits non-zero if any check fails.

The diff can also guide a follow-up prompt or a question to the requirement owner. Mean pairwise :cr across samples gives a disagreement score for each requirement. A Variants node already contains the alternatives needed for a specific clarification, such as “did you mean strictly less than the threshold, or at most?”

With several candidates, cluster equivalent outputs, compare the cluster representatives, and resolve recurring disagreements with validation, replay, examples, or human review.

Get started

Build the engine at the revision used for this post, then run the policy examples. These commands select the revision containing the OpenShell and CEL examples from pull request 103:

git clone https://github.com/yaspar-org/semi-persistent.git
cd semi-persistent
git fetch origin 5a7969ae4ea88117a64faac4f42af5c358e213e2
git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD
cargo build --release        # toolchain auto-pinned; Verus not required

# The worked example from this post:
./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg

# The Dogwood policy-diff example:
./target/release/semi-persistent doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg

# The constructed OpenShell and CEL translation examples:
./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_openshell_policy.egg
./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_cel_policy.egg

# Your own formulas: declare a signature, two terms, and antiunify:
./target/release/semi-persistent MY_PROGRAM.egg

The engine is Apache-2.0 on GitHub. The user guide progresses from basic terms to the policy case studies, and the test suite runs every program in it directly from the repository. Annex B documents the antiunify and checkau commands. If your artifact language has an abstract syntax tree (AST) and an equational theory, you can diff it: Declare the algebra, state the domain identities as rewrites, and ask for the most specific anti-unifier. If your policies are Cedar, whether handwritten or generated for Amazon Verified Permissions, the same recipe applies to them. The OpenShell and CEL examples show how to encode other policy constructs and compare candidate readings of a requirement.

About the authors

item.description: Full title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself.

In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land:

  • A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces.
  • A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint.
  • A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update.

We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it

SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights.

The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary:

CheckWhat it guardsWhy it misses SDC
ECCmemoryCatches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result.
Xid errors (NVRM)GPU driver/hardware faultsThe GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs.
DCGM deep health checkhardware faultsMisses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job.
NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksumstransportVerify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly.
Checkpoint checksumsstorage round-tripA poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine.

The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself.

Solution overview

The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features:

Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas.

Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup.

Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards.

Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window.

Figure 1: A SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster with three p5 nodes running training pods and SDC checks. Node 1 raises an alarm for rank 13, and the proposed steps cordon the node, check GPU metrics, replace it, and restart training

It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different:

LayerSourceWhat it addsCatches truly silent SDC?
1. Non-finite gradient checkYour training scriptNames a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or InfOnly faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow
2. Ring replay auditYour training scriptEvery GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprintsYes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps
3. Weight fingerprint comparisonYour training scriptNames a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the updateYes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights
4. LocalizationYour training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node namesMaps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node namen/a: it localizes
5. DCGM correlationHyperPod observability add-onThe suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarmIt confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node.
6. Deep health checkStartClusterHealthCheck (DCGM L4)An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect nodeIt catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof
7. Repeat-offender historyA query you build over retained alarms and telemetryNodes that alarm repeatedlyPartly: it surfaces nodes worth checking early

Layers 1–3 are the only layers that detect silent SDC, and they live in your training code. Layer 4 turns their alarm into an instance ID, and the HyperPod layers corroborate the alarm and close the loop.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, with at least three GPU nodes. The ring audit needs three different nodes for every comparison it settles, and the weight comparison needs three copies of each weight to name the odd one out. See Orchestrating SageMaker HyperPod clusters with Amazon EKS.
  • A PyTorch DDP training job in which every replica runs its own optimizer step, with a data pipeline that can rebuild any rank’s micro-batch for a given step, such as a seeded sampler.
  • Checkpoints on shared storage, Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Replacing a node destroys its root and secondary volumes, including anything on local NVMe.
  • The SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on for the correlation step. Turn on advanced DCGM metrics if you want ECC, NVLink, and throttling counters.
  • Access to the cluster through kubectl, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for sagemaker:StartClusterHealthCheck and sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes. See Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

Step 1: Detect with three checks in your training loop

Data parallelism trains several copies of the model, called replicas, at the same time. Each replica trains on a different slice of the batch. After each backward pass, an all-reduce averages the replicas’ gradients, and every replica applies that same average in optimizer.step(). Here’s one weight across three replicas, with a learning rate of 0.1:

replica 0replica 1replica 2
weight at start0.5000.5000.500same
local gradient0.200.400.30different (different data)
averaged gradient0.300.300.30same, after the all-reduce
weight after step0.4700.4700.470same

Local gradients differ, because each replica sees different data. And after the optimizer step, the weights must be identical, bit for bit.

Where a fault lands decides which check can see it. If replica 1 computes a local gradient of 4.00 instead of 0.40, the all-reduce spreads that error to every replica: all three apply the same wrong update, and their weights still match. Only replica 1’s local gradient looked different, and only before the all-reduce. If instead replica 1 corrupts a weight during or after the optimizer step, its weights no longer match the others. There’s one exception: a NaN or Inf in one replica’s weights reaches every replica through the next all-reduce, and after that the replicas agree again. A fault inside the all-reduce itself, such as a GPU that adds a partial sum wrong, also reaches every replica identically.

So compute-path faults must be caught before the optimizer step, while the bad gradient can still be discarded, and faults in the update or in stored weights after it. Finite wrong values need recompute: comparing gradient norms across replicas catches only NaN and Inf (see Why not compare local gradient norms?). That gives three checks on every DP rank, in a fixed order within each training step:

  • Non-finite gradient check – Before the all-reduce, flag any rank whose local gradient is NaN or Inf. This catches values that blow up in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step they happen, and names the GPU. After the all-reduce, check the reduced gradient for NaN or Inf too, before the update.
  • Ring replay audit – On audit steps, before the optimizer step, every rank recomputes the micro-batch of a rank on another node. It compares the loss bit for bit and, with deterministic kernels, every parameter’s gradient fingerprint. This catches finite wrong values in the compute path.
  • Weight fingerprint comparison – After the optimizer step, every N steps and before every checkpoint, compare every replica’s weight fingerprints. This catches faults in the optimizer step and in stored weights.

The code in this step is for PyTorch DDP. For tensor, pipeline, or context parallelism, see Beyond DDP.

Order of execution

Figure 2: Flowchart of one training step. Check 1 (NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce) and check 2 (ring replay, on audit steps) run before the optimizer step and stop the step if they fire. Check 3 (weight fingerprints) runs after it and blocks the checkpoint

Why not compare local gradient norms?

A natural first design, and the one we started with, flags a rank whose local gradient norm is more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median of that step. We recorded every rank’s local gradient norm on every step of the three fault-free runs on 4 instances (22,800 steps, see Fault-free runs) on 32 H100s training a 953-million-parameter model, and the test doesn’t work:

  • The healthy spread is too wide – Each rank sees different data, so healthy local norms already reached 224 MADs in the first 800 steps, and 1,240 MADs over all healthy steps.
  • A quiet threshold sees nothing finite – At k = 336, 1.5 times the highest score in the first 800 healthy steps, it raised 11 false alarms in the remaining 22,000 healthy steps. And no finite fault came close: the faulty rank’s score never exceeded 6.9, even with one activation multiplied by 10,000.

Compare by fingerprint

Checks 2 and 3 compare tensors across GPUs. Sending whole tensors would cost too much, so each tensor is reduced to a fingerprint: two 64-bit sums of its raw bit patterns, one plain and one weighted by position. Any change to one or two elements of a tensor changes the fingerprint, for tensors with fewer than 2³² elements of up to 4 bytes each. That covers every weight fault we injected. Larger changes could, in principle, cancel out, so equal fingerprints are strong evidence of equal tensors, not proof. The position-weighted sum matters: in our tests, a swap of two weight values and a compensating change to two values left the plain sum unchanged, and only the weighted sum caught them.

_INT_VIEW = {1: torch.uint8, 2: torch.int16, 4: torch.int32, 8: torch.int64}

@torch.no_grad()
def fingerprints(tensors, chunk=1 << 24):
    # ... picks the device and allocates out: one row of two int64 per tensor
    for k, t in enumerate(tensors):
        if t is None:
            continue
        bits = t.detach().contiguous().view(-1).view(_INT_VIEW[t.element_size()])
        for i in range(0, bits.numel(), chunk):  # chunked to bound temporary memory
            b = bits[i:i + chunk].to(torch.int64)
            pos = torch.arange(i + 1, i + 1 + b.numel(), dtype=torch.int64, device=dev)
            out[k, 0] += b.sum()
            out[k, 1] += (b * pos).sum()
    return out

Check 1: NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce

A DDP communication hook records each rank’s local gradient before it’s averaged. It stores the squared norm of every gradient bucket and, on deterministic audit steps, the fingerprints of every parameter’s gradient (used by check 2). Then it passes the bucket to PyTorch’s standard all-reduce.

After backward, nonfinite_ranks gathers one scalar from every rank and returns the ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf. The first rank flagged is the faulty one. If the step were applied, the NaN would reach every rank on the next step.

def local_stats_hook(stats, bucket):
    stats.sq.append(bucket.buffer().float().pow(2).sum())
    if stats.record_fingerprints:  # per parameter, before allreduce_hook divides in place
        rows = [stats.row[p.data_ptr()] for p in bucket.parameters()]
        stats.fp[rows] = fingerprints(bucket.gradients())
    return allreduce_hook(stats.dp_group, bucket)

def attach(ddp_model, dp_group):
    stats = LocalStats(dp_group, list(ddp_model.module.parameters()))
    ddp_model.register_comm_hook(state=stats, hook=local_stats_hook)
    return stats

def nonfinite_ranks(stats):
    """After backward: global ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf."""
    local = torch.stack(stats.sq).sum().sqrt().reshape(1)
    n = dist.get_world_size(stats.dp_group)
    gathered = [torch.empty_like(local) for _ in range(n)]
    dist.all_gather(gathered, local, group=stats.dp_group)
    bad = ~torch.isfinite(torch.cat(gathered).cpu())
    return [dist.get_global_rank(stats.dp_group, r) for r in bad.nonzero().flatten().tolist()]

train() also checks the gradient after the all-reduce. A NaN or Inf produced inside the reduction reaches every replica the same way, so the copies still match and check 3 passes them. Without this check, the NaN becomes NaN weights on every replica, and a checkpoint due on that step is saved with them and tagged as passing. clip_grad_norm_ already computes the norm of the reduced gradient, so the check adds only one one-element all-reduce per step. A finite error in the reduction still passes every check.

If you train with fp16 and a gradient scaler, exclude the overflow steps the scaler already skips. bf16 doesn’t have them.

Check 2: Ring replay, before the optimizer step

Every replica holds the same weights until optimizer.step(). So, between the backward pass and the optimizer step, any rank can recompute any other rank’s micro-batch, and with deterministic kernels it must get the same bits.

On an audit step, every rank r recomputes the micro-batch of rank r + 8: 8 positions ahead, which is one node away on p5 instances. It uses the unwrapped module, so nothing is all-reduced, and it restores the gradients, the module’s buffers, and the random-number state afterwards. A replay blocks the job no matter how many ranks do one, so auditing every rank costs the same wall-clock time as auditing one.

Each rank then appears in two comparisons: its own micro-batch, replayed by a peer, and the micro-batch it replayed for someone else.

  • Both comparisons mismatch: That rank computed wrong in both, so it’s the culprit.
  • Only one mismatches: Either side could be wrong. confirm settles it in place: the GPU eight positions after the target, on a third node, and the target itself replay the target’s micro-batch again. That also tells a persistent fault, which the target reproduces, from a transient one, which it doesn’t.
def ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats, local_loss, offset, with_grads):
    # ... g is the DP group, n its size, and me this rank's position in it
    target = dist.get_global_rank(g, (me + offset) % n)
    replay = _replay(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch(step, target), with_grads)
    # ... v = [this rank's own loss bits and gradient fingerprints, its replay of target]
    dist.all_gather_into_tensor(out, v, group=g)
    table = out.view(n, 2, -1).cpu()  # per DP rank: [own result, its replay of its target]
    pairs = [(dist.get_global_rank(g, (r + offset) % n), dist.get_global_rank(g, r))
             for r in range(n) if not torch.equal(table[(r + offset) % n, 0], table[r, 1])]
    return pairs, table

def localize(pairs):
    hits = Counter(r for p in pairs for r in p)
    culprits = sorted(r for r, c in hits.items() if c >= 2)
    ambiguous = [p for p in pairs if not set(p) & set(culprits)]
    return culprits, ambiguous

def confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, pair, table, stats, offset, with_grads):
    # ... the third GPU (target + offset) and the target replay the target's micro-batch again
    third_r, self_r = v.cpu()
    orig, peer = table[ti, 0], table[ri, 1]
    if torch.equal(third_r, orig):
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": replayer, "kind": "replayer computed wrong"}
    if torch.equal(third_r, peer):
        kind = ("persistent" if torch.equal(self_r, orig) else
                "transient" if torch.equal(self_r, third_r) else "unclear")
        return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": target, "kind": kind}
    return {"pair": pair, "third": third, "suspect": None, "kind": "unattributable"}

The confirmation is only independent if the three GPUs are on three different nodes. check_topology verifies that for every pair before training starts, from each pod’s NODE_NAME, and raises an error otherwise.

Choose the audit mode:

  • Default kernels: Compare the loss only. This needs a forward pass whose loss is bitwise reproducible, which held in our tests: healthy replays matched the original loss bit for bit. Gradients can’t be compared this way, because attention’s default backward pass isn’t deterministic. This mode catches forward-pass faults that change the loss.
  • Deterministic kernels (deterministic_audits=True): The whole audit step runs with deterministic algorithms and the math attention kernel. Gradient fingerprints then match too, so the audit also catches backward-only faults. An op with no deterministic implementation raises an error instead of producing a false alarm. On our model, a deterministic audit step cost 2.4 times a default one.

Never replay a suspect’s work on the suspect alone. A GPU with a persistent defect can reproduce its own wrong answer.

Check 3: Weight fingerprints, after the optimizer step

After optimizer.step(), every replica’s weights must be identical, so there’s no tolerance to tune. Each rank fingerprints every weight tensor and gathers everyone’s fingerprints.

A rank is named only when its copy of a tensor differs from a strict majority, more than half of the copies. With two copies, or a split with no strict majority, the comparison reports a disagreement without naming any rank.

def find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group):
    local = fingerprints(params).flatten()
    # ... all-gathers every rank's fingerprints into table: [dp_size, num_tensors, 2]
    differs = (table != table[0]).any(dim=2).any(dim=0)
    if not differs.any():
        return {"diverged": False, "suspects": []}
    suspects = set()
    for k in differs.nonzero().flatten().tolist():
        copies = [tuple(row) for row in table[:, k].tolist()]
        value, count = Counter(copies).most_common(1)[0]
        if 2 * count <= n:
            return {"diverged": True, "suspects": None}  # no strict majority for tensor k
        suspects.update(r for r, c in enumerate(copies) if c != value)
    return {"diverged": True,
            "suspects": sorted(dist.get_global_rank(dp_group, r) for r in suspects)}

Run it every N steps and on every checkpoint step. It’s the only check that runs after the update, so it’s the only one that can stop a checkpoint from being written out of a corrupted copy. In our tests, a weight corrupted right after one update was caught at the next checkpoint step, and the save didn’t happen. Without the forced check, the save went ahead from the corrupted copy, and the ring audit noticed only at the next audit, five steps later.

It costs 31.1 ms per check on a 953-million-parameter model: 2 percent of a step when it runs every 10 steps.

Put the checks in the training loop

train runs each step in the order of Figure 2 and stops at the first alarm. It decides whether a step is an audit step before the forward pass, because a deterministic comparison needs the original computation to be deterministic too. When check 1 or 2 fires, it zeros the gradients and returns without clipping or applying the update, so the bad gradient never reaches the weights or the optimizer state, and the exact state is still there for confirmation. After clipping, it checks whether the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf, and if it is, returns before the update. It saves a checkpoint only if nothing fired.

def train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, save_checkpoint,
          sched, start_step=0):
    # ... setup, including check_topology(dp_group, sched.peer_offset)
    for step, batch in enumerate(batches, start_step):
        audit = step % sched.audit_every == 0  # 0. decide first
        det = audit and sched.deterministic_audits
        # ... resets the hook's per-step state
        with deterministic() if det else nullcontext():
            loss = compute_loss(ddp_model, batch)  # 1. forward, backward
            loss.backward()
        nonfinite = nonfinite_ranks(stats)  # 2. non-finite check
        pairs, table = [], None
        if audit or nonfinite:  # 3. ring replay
            pairs, table = ring_audit(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, stats,
                                      loss, sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det)
        if nonfinite or pairs:  # 4. gate
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            culprits, ambiguous = localize(pairs)
            verdicts = [confirm(module, compute_loss, rebuild_batch, step, p, table, stats,
                                sched.peer_offset, with_grads=det) for p in ambiguous]
            return {"step": step, "check": "compute", "nonfinite": nonfinite,
                    "mismatched_pairs": pairs, "culprits": culprits, "verdicts": verdicts,
                    "suspect_window": _window(last_audit, step, start_step),
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        if audit:
            last_audit = step
        grad_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, sched.max_grad_norm)
        bad = (~torch.isfinite(grad_norm)).to(torch.int32).reshape(1)  # reduced gradient
        dist.all_reduce(bad, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=dp_group)
        if bad.item():
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # step not applied
            return {"step": step, "check": "reduced gradient", "suspect_window": [step, step],
                    "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        ckpt = step % sched.ckpt_every == 0
        if step % sched.check_every == 0 or (ckpt and sched.check_on_checkpoint):
            wc = find_divergent_ranks(params, dp_group)  # 5. weight check
            if wc["diverged"]:
                return {"step": step, "check": "weights", "suspects": wc["suspects"],
                        "suspect_window": _window(last_weights, step, start_step),
                        "last_audit_pass": last_audit, "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights}
            last_weights = step
        if ckpt:  # 6. checkpoint
            save_checkpoint(step, tags={"last_audit_pass": last_audit,
                                        "last_weight_check_pass": last_weights})
    return None

The alarm’s suspect_window is the range of steps since the last pass of the check that fired. A fault that was active on every step since it started began inside it. An intermittent fault can be older, and a fault that no check sees can be in any checkpoint, so treat the tags as a record that the checks passed at that step, not as proof that the saved state is clean.

A training script calls it like this:

# ... imports, and the model, optimizer, and dataset setup
import sdc_order as S

stats = S.attach(ddp_model, dp_group)  # registers the comm hook, once
sched = S.Schedule(audit_every=10, deterministic_audits=True, check_every=10,
                   ckpt_every=100, peer_offset=8)  # 8 = GPUs per node

def compute_loss(model, batch):  # used for training AND replay
    x, y = batch
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits = model(x)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.float().flatten(0, 1), y.flatten())

def rebuild_batch(step, rank):  # exactly the micro-batch `rank` trained on
    return dataset.micro_batch(step, rank)

# ... batches(start) yields this rank's micro-batches and sets the learning rate
alarm = S.train(ddp_model, stats, optimizer, batches(start), compute_loss, rebuild_batch,
                save_checkpoint, sched, start_step=start)
if alarm is not None:
    report_sdc(alarm)  # metric + log line; Step 2 maps the rank to a node
    sys.exit(3)

The replay depends on these:

  • Exact micro-batches: rebuild_batch(step, rank) must return exactly the micro-batch that rank trained on, for example from a seeded sampler.
  • Same loss function: compute_loss must be the same function in training and in replay, including autocast, and any randomness inside it, such as dropout, must be seeded per step and rank.
  • No collectives or output-affecting state in the model: The confirmation replay runs on only two ranks, the target and the third GPU, so a model that calls a collective inside its forward or backward pass (SyncBatchNorm, for example) hangs on an ambiguous alarm. A buffer that the forward pass both reads and updates makes a healthy replay differ.
  • Deterministic setup: Set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 before the training process starts, and make sure every op in the model has a deterministic implementation.
  • Peer offset: Number DP ranks node by node, so that peer_offset equal to the GPUs per node puts every replayer on another node. check_topology refuses a layout where it doesn’t.
  • Untested here: Unused parameters, gradient accumulation, BatchNorm, and forward hooks with side effects. With unused parameters, set deterministic_audits=False, which compares the loss only.

audit_every is the main cost-versus-robustness setting:

  • Detection delay: A persistent finite fault is caught within audit_every steps if it also occurs in the kernels the audit runs. Deterministic audits run deterministic kernels and the math attention kernel, so a fault confined to the default kernels used on the other steps is never audited.
  • Corrupted updates: Up to audit_every − 1 corrupted updates can be applied before the audit catches it. They’re inside the alarm’s suspect_window.
  • One-time faults: A finite fault on a single non-audit step that doesn’t recur isn’t caught at all.

Make ckpt_every a multiple of both audit_every and check_every, so every checkpoint step is audited before its update and fingerprinted after it.

We measured the average step time end to end, over 1,000 consecutive steps per schedule, on the 953M model and 32 H100s. Every schedule with the checks also runs the weight check every 10 steps:

ScheduleAverage step timeOver plain DDP
Plain DDP, no checks157.4 ms—
Checks, no audits169.0 ms+7.4%
Deterministic audits every 10 steps211.9 ms+34.7%
Default-kernel audits every 10 steps177.0 ms+12.5%
Deterministic audits every 100 steps173.3 ms+10.1%
Default-kernel audits every 100 steps169.3 ms+7.6%

About 7 percentage points of each schedule’s cost don’t depend on audits: the gradient hook and the two NaN/Inf checks on every step, and the weight check every 10 steps. A reasonable starting point for production is deterministic audits every 100 steps, which cost 10 percent here. They still catch a persistent fault within 100 steps, including a backward-only one, at the price of up to 99 corrupted updates to roll back. Audit every 10 steps when you need faster detection, for example during a burn-in on new capacity or while you watch a suspect node. Measure the cost on your own model: deterministic attention uses the math kernel, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

In the fault-free runs, 15,320 audit steps and 3,080 weight checks raised no alarm, which bounds the false-alarm rate at about 1 in 5,100 audit steps (95 percent confidence).

Step 2: Localize the suspect rank to a node

A rank is a logical ID. To act on it, you need the instance and the physical GPU. On HyperPod EKS, the Kubernetes node name is the instance ID with a hyperpod- prefix. Pass it to your pod with the Kubernetes downward API:

env:
- name: NODE_NAME  # on HyperPod EKS, spec.nodeName is "hyperpod-<instance-id>"
  valueFrom:
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: spec.nodeName

At job start, log a table that maps every rank to its node, instance, and GPU UUID:

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

node = os.environ["NODE_NAME"]  # "hyperpod-i-0123456789abcdef0"
instance_id = node.removeprefix("hyperpod-")  # "i-0123456789abcdef0", what the Replace API takes
gpu_uuid = "GPU-" + str(torch.cuda.get_device_properties(torch.cuda.current_device()).uuid)
info = {"rank": dist.get_rank(), "node": node,
        "instance_id": instance_id, "gpu_uuid": gpu_uuid}
table = [None] * dist.get_world_size()
dist.all_gather_object(table, info)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    print("rank_map", table)  # log at every job start

If a job is already running without the downward API, you can map a pod to its node from outside with kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'.

Step 3: Contain the damage and check the GPU metrics

When an alarm fires, stop the job first. Then stop new work from landing on the suspect node by cordoning the node while you investigate:

kubectl cordon <node-name>  # marks the node unschedulable; existing pods keep running

Then open the GPU health dashboard in the SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on, filter to the suspect node and GPU, and look at the time the alarm fired. A rise in correctable ECC errors, PCIe replays, throttling, or temperature on that GPU raises confidence that the hardware is at fault. A clean panel doesn’t clear the node: pure SDC often leaves no trace in hardware telemetry.

Step 4: Confirm, then replace the node

With the Step 1 checks running, an alarm already names a suspect GPU. When you see a symptom without an alarm, such as a loss spike, or want to rule out software before you replace anything, start with the cheap explanations. Most loss spikes aren’t SDC, and chasing SDC on a data bug wastes days:

Loss anomaly / suspected corruption
- Reproduces with the same seed on DIFFERENT nodes? -> deterministic bug, not SDC
- Goes away, or follows one node, when you move the job? -> strong SDC candidate
- DP replicas that must be bitwise identical disagree? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's step replayed on another node gives different bits? -> strong SDC signal
- One rank's pre-all-reduce gradient is NaN or Inf? -> SDC candidate (use the first step it fired)
- Fleet-wide and gradual? -> likely recipe or optimizer
- Started at a data, config, or library change? -> usually software, but not proof

The test that separates SDC from software is whether the problem follows the hardware:

  • A reproducible failure doesn’t rule out SDC – Meta pinned a failing workload to one core and got the same wrong answer every time for specific inputs.
  • Neither does a failure that starts at a software change – Google traced one incident to a correct library update that began using rarely used instructions on defective cores.
  • Don’t expect the global loss to point anywhere – A forward fault first changes the faulty rank’s own loss, and the all-reduce then spreads its gradient to every replica. Per-rank checks and replays give you the locality.

Decide what the alarm means

AlarmMeaningSuggested action
check == "weights", suspects == [r]Rank r’s copy differs from a strict majority after the updateKeep r’s node cordoned. Replace it after review
check == "weights", suspects is NoneCopies disagree, but no strict majorityAmbiguous: keep the nodes involved cordoned. Check DCGM and run deep health checks
culprits == [r]Both of r’s ring comparisons mismatched. This assumes at most one faulty GPU among the GPUs that replay each other (the GPUs with the same local index). With two, a healthy GPU can be namedKeep cordoned. Replace after review, or after the fault repeats
Verdict persistentThe target reproduced its own wrong answer, and a third GPU agreed with the replayerKeep cordoned. Replace after review
Verdict transientThe target’s retry came out right and agreed with the third GPU. An intermittent fault can look the sameKeep cordoned until an audit with the node as the target, or a deep health check, passes. Replace it if it happens again
Verdict replayer computed wrongThe replaying GPU, not the target, was wrongTreat the replayer as the suspect, and confirm again
nonfinite set, no mismatched pairsNaN or Inf in a backward pass that the loss doesn’t show, or a gradient norm too large for float32 (above about 1.8 × 10¹⁹)Ambiguous: audit with the suspect as the target, or check DCGM and run a deep health check
check == "reduced gradient"The gradient was NaN or Inf after the all-reduce, although every rank’s local gradient was finite. No rank is namedAmbiguous: keep the job stopped, check DCGM and run deep health checks on every node in the job, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the alarm step
Verdict unattributable or unclearThe three GPUs don’t line upAmbiguous: check DCGM and run deep health checks on the nodes involved

In production, keep a human approval on every replacement until you have evidence of the checks’ precision on your own workload. Synthetic tests like ours don’t establish it.

Confirm an ambiguous alarm

A deep health check is the main tool for ambiguous alarms. Its stress tests catch faults that the hardware reports, and subtle data-dependent faults often pass. To run one on the suspect instance group:

aws sagemaker start-cluster-health-check \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --deep-health-check-configurations '[{"InstanceGroupName":"<instance-group>","InstanceIds":["i-0123456789abcdef0"],"DeepHealthChecks":["InstanceStress"]}]'

Replace the node

When you’re ready to replace the node, you have two options. Both trigger the same SageMaker HyperPod recovery process, described in Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

If automatic node recovery is turned on, you can label the node and let SageMaker HyperPod replace it, which is convenient for automation:

kubectl label node <node-name> \
    sagemaker.amazonaws.com/node-health-status=UnschedulablePendingReplacement --overwrite

To use the API instead, run:

aws sagemaker batch-replace-cluster-nodes --cluster-name <cluster-name> --node-ids <instance-id>

On clusters that use Karpenter for autoscaling, BatchReplaceClusterNodes terminates the node but creates a replacement only if pending pods need one. After the replacement joins, the training job restarts through the SageMaker HyperPod training operator or the job’s restart policy, and your training script resumes from the newest checkpoint saved before the alarm’s suspect_window starts. Call find_divergent_ranks right after loading it, before the first step. Replacement destroys the node’s root and secondary volumes, so keep checkpoints on shared storage.

Automating the workflow

The manual steps are for understanding. In production, wrap them in a small controller that runs in your own cluster and account:

  • Trigger: The training job reports the alarm as a Kubernetes event, a small custom resource (for example SDCReport{rank, job, step, check}), or an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on metrics such as sdc_nonfinite_grad, sdc_replay_mismatch, and sdc_divergent_tensors.
  • Resolve: The controller maps rank → pod → node through the Kubernetes API, then node → instance ID by stripping the hyperpod- prefix.
  • Contain: It cordons the node.
  • Decide: It applies the table in Step 4. The ring audit has already confirmed ambiguous pairs in place, so the alarm carries the verdicts. For an ambiguous result, it runs one node-scoped deep health check.
  • Recover: For a replacement, it asks a human to approve, then calls BatchReplaceClusterNodes, or sets the node-health label if automatic node recovery is turned on. Then it relies on the training operator and your checkpoint reload, and records every step in CloudWatch.

Build it as a lightweight Kubernetes operator, or as an Amazon EventBridge rule on the CloudWatch alarm that invokes an AWS Lambda function.

Use case: Testing the checks on SageMaker HyperPod

We ran the tests twice on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, using 4 and then 3 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs each, and PyTorch 2.9.0 (CUDA 13.0) from the AWS Deep Learning Containers training image. The model was a 953-million-parameter Llama-style decoder with 16 layers, a hidden size of 2,048, 16 attention heads, a 32,000-token vocabulary, and 2,048-token sequences. Each GPU processed 2 sequences per step (131,072 tokens per step on 32 GPUs), with fp32 weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and bf16 autocast for compute. We trained with AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ after a 100-step linear warm-up, with betas of (0.9, 0.95), weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The data was synthetic: a copy task with Zipf-distributed tokens whose first half repeats, seeded per rank and step so that any micro-batch can be rebuilt.

Fault scenarios

Faults were injected in one layer, the MLP down-projection of the eighth of 16 decoder blocks, on a chosen rank and step:

  • Forward faults change the layer’s output but keep its gradient path, like a wrong multiply in the forward pass.
  • Backward-only faults change the gradient of the layer’s input or weight.
  • Weight faults change one GPU’s copy of the stored weight right after the optimizer step: a bit flip, a swap of two values, or a compensating change to two values.
  • A persistent fault recurs in everything the faulty GPU computes, including the replays it runs for other ranks. A transient fault fires once.

Every scenario restarts from a snapshot taken after 400 warm-up steps, and step numbers count from it. Unless noted, audits ran every 10 steps with deterministic kernels, weight checks every 10 steps, and a checkpoint every 20. The table shows the 4-instance results. On 3 instances, every scenario raised the same alarm, at the same step, from the same check, naming the same ranks. Only the peer ranks changed.

Injected faultResultCaught by
NaN in one element of rank 13’s forward output, on step 25 only (not an audit step)Fired on step 25 and named rank 13. The ring replay also ran. Confirmation by rank 21 and rank 13: transient on rank 13. Step 25 wasn’t applied. Suspect window: steps 21–25Check 1
One element of rank 13’s forward output ×1,000, on every step from step 23Steps 23–29 passed check 1 and were applied. The audit at step 30 mismatched (13, 5) and (21, 13) and named rank 13. Step 30 wasn’t applied. Suspect window: steps 21–30Check 2
The same ×1,000 on audit step 30 onlyOne pair mismatched, (13, 5). Confirmation by rank 21, on a third node, and by rank 13: transient on rank 13Check 2
The persistent ×1,000 on rank 5, which replays rank 13’s micro-batchPairs (13, 5) and (5, 29) mismatched. Named rank 5. A single replay of rank 13 by rank 5 would have blamed the healthy rank 13Check 2
Other forward faults on rank 13, every step from step 23: one element ×10,000, 10% multiplicative noise on the whole output, bit 3 flipped in one bf16 element, and one output column ×1.1Each named rank 13 at step 30. The bit flip and the ×1.1 column were also caught with default-kernel auditsCheck 2
One element of the gradient flowing into rank 13’s layer, or of its weight gradient, ×1,000, every step from step 23 (backward only)Each named rank 13 at step 30, from the gradient fingerprints aloneCheck 2
The weight-gradient fault above, with default-kernel auditsNo alarm in 50 steps. The checkpoints at steps 20 and 40 were tagged with passing audits and weight checks, because the loss was unaffected and every copy had applied the same corrupted updatesNot caught
The persistent forward ×1,000 on ranks 13 and 22 at oncePairs (13, 5), (21, 13), (22, 14) and (30, 22) mismatched. Named ranks 13 and 22Check 2
Bit 22 flipped in one fp32 weight element on rank 0 after the step-31 update, with a checkpoint every 5 stepsThe forced weight check at checkpoint step 35 named rank 0, and the save didn’t happen. Suspect window: steps 31–35Check 3
The same, with check_on_checkpoint=FalseThe save at step 35 went ahead from rank 0’s corrupted copy. Its tags showed the last passing weight check at step 30. The ring audit named rank 0 at step 40, from pairs (8, 0) and (0, 24)Check 2
Two values swapped, or +4,096 and −4,096 added to the bit patterns of two values, in one weight tensor on rank 0 after the step-31 update, with no audits and weight checks every 10 stepsEach named rank 0 at the step-40 weight check, although the tensor’s plain bit sum hadn’t changedCheck 3
Bit 22 flipped in one attention weight on rank 7, after restoring the snapshot (a stand-in for loading a checkpoint)find_divergent_ranks, run before the first step, named rank 7Check 3

Fault-free runs

To measure false alarms, we trained without faults on both cluster sizes, with three schedules each. Every schedule ran the weight check every 10 steps and saved no checkpoints, and each run’s length was fixed in minutes, so the two schedules that audit every step contribute most of the audit steps:

InstancesAuditsMinutesStepsAudit stepsWeight checksAlarms
4Deterministic, every step454,6004,6004600
4Default kernels, every step22.55,4005,4005400
4Deterministic, every 10 steps4512,8001,2801,2800
3Deterministic, every step151,6001,6001600
3Default kernels, every step7.52,0002,0002000
3Deterministic, every 10 steps154,4004404400
Total15030,80015,3203,0800

With 0 alarms in 15,320 audit steps, the rule of three puts a 95 percent upper bound of 3 / 15,320, about 1 in 5,100, on the false-alarm rate per audit step. The NaN/Inf checks didn’t fire on any fault-free step either. The gradient-norm analysis in Why not compare local gradient norms? uses the 4-instance runs only.

Beyond DDP

The weight comparison isn’t limited to DDP. find_divergent_ranks takes any data-parallel group, so it also applies to tensor, pipeline, and context parallelism, HSDP, and mixture of experts, which are all layouts that keep independent copies of each weight. It can’t help under ZeRO-1 or full FSDP sharding, where each shard’s update is computed on only one rank. We tested the checks and the training loop in this post only with DDP.

To use it in another layout, call find_divergent_ranks with the group that holds copies of the same shard. With only two copies, it can detect a disagreement but can’t name the faulty copy.

If you’d rather have the service check your nodes for you, SageMaker HyperPod also offers the MultiNodeTraining deep health check. It runs a short, fixed distributed training job across a batch of GPU nodes, with no code changes, and replaces nodes whose training loss turns NaN or Inf, diverges, or doesn’t finish in time. Select it alongside InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity when you create an instance group, or run it on demand with StartClusterHealthCheck. It complements the checks in this post: use it to screen new and replacement nodes before your job lands on them, and the in-job checks to catch wrong values in your own training that never become NaN or Inf. For details, visit SageMaker HyperPod Deep Health Checks.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete what you created for testing. If you created a HyperPod cluster, delete it with aws sagemaker delete-cluster --cluster-name <cluster-name>. That removes only the HyperPod resources. Delete the EKS cluster, its add-ons, and any Amazon FSx volumes separately, after the HyperPod cluster. See Deleting a SageMaker HyperPod cluster.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to detect silent data corruption in data-parallel training and how to hand a suspect node to SageMaker HyperPod for replacement. Three checks cover the three places a fault can land: a NaN/Inf check on each rank’s gradient and on the reduced gradient, a ring replay that compares every GPU’s work with a GPU on another node, and a weight fingerprint comparison after the update. Run the first two before the optimizer step, don’t apply a step that failed a check, and compare weights before every checkpoint. Node names on SageMaker HyperPod EKS clusters turn the suspect rank into an instance ID. Then quarantine the node, roll back to a checkpoint from before the suspect window, and let the node-health label or the Replace API complete the recovery.

To get started, review the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency features for Amazon EKS, and try the companion repository. To go deeper, see deep health checks and the observability add-on.

About the authors

item.title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results.

Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline.

Why a standalone API?

The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions. But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit:

  • Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway.
  • Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure.
  • Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway.
  • Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack.

The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation.

How it works

The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage.

Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows

The numbered steps are:

  • Your application calls InvokeWebSearch with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint.
  • The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the AWS managed web search tool.
  • The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range.
  • The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine.
  • The API returns up to maxResults ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time.

The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "InvokeWebSearch",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1"
        }
    ]
}

A first search request

The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3):

import boto3

client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2")

response = client.invoke_web_search(
    webSearchId="web-search.v1",
    searchQuery="multi-region EKS cluster deployment best practices",
    maxResults=10,
    filters={
        "domainFilter": {"include": ["aws.amazon.com", "kubernetes.io"]},
        "publishedDateFilter": {"publishedAfter": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"},
    },
)

for result in response["results"]:
    print(result.get("publishedAt"), result.get("title"), result.get("url"))

Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with get. One result from a live call, shortened:

{
    "title": "One Amazon EKS, many edges: How to choose your edge container strategy on AWS",
    "url": "https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/one-amazon-eks-many-edges-how-to-choose-your-edge-container-strategy-on-aws/",
    "text": "Separate the standard from the deployment model Choosing the wrong platform isn't really the issue. ...",
    "publishedAt": "2026-09-25T15:52:00Z"
}

That’s the full integration. If your code runs on AWS Lambda, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the execution role provides credentials automatically. Add the permission to that role, and the same code runs unchanged.

Key API features

  • Domain filtering – Include or exclude specific domains to scope search results to trusted sources (for example, only aws.amazon.com and kubernetes.io for an assistant focused on AWS). Each list holds up to 100 domain names, and a root domain also matches its subdomains.
  • Date filtering – Restrict results to a publication time range with publishedAfter and publishedBefore, given as RFC 3339 date-times in UTC such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z. Both bounds are inclusive.
  • Configurable result count – Request between 1 and 25 results per query. If you don’t set maxResults, the API returns up to 25. The search text, searchQuery, can be up to 200 characters.
  • Results with text extracts – Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time, ready to feed into your model’s context window.

Getting started in under 5 minutes

Here are two ways to get a first result:

Option 1: AWS CloudShell (no local setup)

  • Open AWS CloudShell in your browser. It uses the credentials of your console session.
  • Your role will have the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch permission, from the preceding policy or from the broader AWS managed policy BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess.
  • Run: aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-web-search \ --web-search-id web-search.v1 \ --search-query "latest EKS features" \ --max-results 5

Option 2: Local development

  • Install the AWS CLI, or the AWS SDK for your language. For Python, use Boto3 1.43.127 or later.
  • Create an IAM role with the preceding policy.
  • Get credentials for that role: assume it from your application or an AWS CLI profile, or sign in with it through your identity provider.
  • Run the preceding Python example, or call the API from any AWS SDK.

There’s no resource to create and no API key to manage. Authenticate, call, and get results.

Using the Web Search API with agent frameworks

The Web Search API fits naturally into popular agent frameworks. LangChain agents get it through the AgentCore web search tool in langchain-aws 1.9.3 and later:

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_aws.tools import create_web_search_toolkit

toolkit, tools = create_web_search_toolkit(region="us-west-2")
model = init_chat_model("bedrock_converse:us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5", region_name="us-west-2")
agent = create_agent(model, tools=tools, system_prompt="Cite the URL of every fact you use.")

The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as domains to exclude, a date floor, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. For a complete example, see the daily dependency watch sample. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel with LangGraph, and checks every finding against its sources before it reports anything.

If you prefer to wrap the call yourself, a plain LangChain tool works too:

from langchain.tools import tool
import boto3
import json

client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2")

@tool
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the web for current information."""
    response = client.invoke_web_search(
        webSearchId="web-search.v1",
        searchQuery=query,
        maxResults=5,
    )
    return json.dumps(response["results"], indent=2, default=str)

# Pass web_search to an agent, for example create_agent(model, tools=[web_search])

Without a framework, the WebSearchClient in the AgentCore Python SDK wraps the same call and returns results with parsed dates. langchain-aws 1.9.3 and the AgentCore Python SDK 1.26.0 add Web Search API support, so install those versions or later.

Enterprise controls, built in

Because the Web Search API uses standard IAM authentication, you get enterprise controls from the first call:

  • IAM policies. Grant or deny bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch per user, group, or role. Use service control policies (SCPs) to enforce guardrails across accounts.
  • AWS CloudTrail logging. CloudTrail records InvokeWebSearch requests as data events. Data events aren’t logged by default, so add an event selector for the AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WebSearch resource type to a trail or event data store. Events record the web search tool and maxResults, not the search text or filters. For details, see Log AgentCore Web Search API calls with AWS CloudTrail.
  • VPC support. Use AWS PrivateLink to route API calls over your private network rather than the public internet. For setup and endpoint policies, see Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink later in this post.
  • Compliance. For a list of compliance programs that cover AgentCore, see Compliance validation for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Searches stay in AWS. Queries are served from a web index that Amazon operates and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine.
  • Acceptable use. For details, see the Web Search API Acceptable Use documentation.

Quotas apply per account. For the defaults and how to request an increase, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

By default, each account can send up to 10 requests per second in each Region, and you can request an increase. For details, see AgentCore Web Search Service Quotas.

Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink

Agents and pipelines that handle sensitive data often run in private subnets with no route to the internet. With AWS PrivateLink, that code can call the Web Search API through an interface VPC endpoint in your VPC. Traffic between your VPC and the API stays on the AWS network, and you don’t need an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a proxy to reach it.

Figure 2: Calling the Web Search API through AWS PrivateLink

The numbered steps are:

  • Your application calls InvokeWebSearch at the API’s standard Regional name. With private DNS, that name resolves to the interface endpoint in your subnet.
  • The endpoint policy applies, and the request reaches the API over the AWS network.
  • The API checks with IAM that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch, including any aws:SourceVpce condition.
  • The API applies the request’s filters and searches the Amazon-operated web index.
  • The results return through the endpoint to your application.

To set it up, create an interface endpoint for the AgentCore data plane service, com.amazonaws.<Region>.bedrock-agentcore, in each VPC and Region that calls the API, and turn on private DNS:

aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
    --region us-west-2 \
    --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
    --service-name com.amazonaws.us-west-2.bedrock-agentcore \
    --subnet-ids subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-0fedcba9876543210 \
    --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --private-dns-enabled

With private DNS turned on, the API’s standard Regional name, bedrock-agentcore.us-west-2.amazonaws.com, resolves to the endpoint’s private IP addresses inside your VPC. The Boto3 and AWS CLI examples in this post run unchanged, with no endpoint URL to set. The endpoint’s security group must allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the resources that call the API.

PrivateLink also gives you controls on top of IAM:

  • Endpoint policies – A VPC endpoint policy applies to InvokeWebSearch requests in addition to your IAM policies, so you decide which principals can search through the endpoint. The same endpoint also carries the other AgentCore data plane APIs, such as AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Memory, Identity, Browser, and Code Interpreter. If workloads in the VPC call them too, add statements that allow those calls. The following policy lets only one role call the API through the endpoint: { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/WebSearchAppRole" }, "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1" }
  • Require the private path – Add an aws:SourceVpce condition to the IAM policy that grants the permission. The role can then search only through your endpoint, and the same call from outside the VPC is denied: { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceVpce": "vpce-0123456789abcdef0" } } }
  • Network-level control – Security groups and subnet placement decide which instances, containers, and functions can reach the endpoint at all.

PrivateLink works the same way in every Region where the Web Search API is available. Interface endpoints are billed at standard AWS PrivateLink pricing. For details, see Call AgentCore Web Search through AWS PrivateLink.

Try it in the console

You can try the Web Search API in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console before you write any code. In the navigation pane, under Connections, choose Web Search.

Figure 3: Web Search in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console

  • Configure. In the Configure panel, set: Max results: how many results each query returns, from 1–25. The console starts at 10. Published date: a date range in YYYY/MM/DD format. Only results published inside it come back. Leave it empty to include results from any date. Domain filtering: up to 100 domains to include and up to 100 to exclude. Choose View and manage domains to edit the lists.
  • Test. Enter a query of up to 200 characters in the Test Web Search API panel. Each query calls the Web Search API with your settings. The panel shows how many results came back and how long the call took. For each result it shows the title, a text snippet, the publication date and the source URL. Figure 4 shows a search for “How do I set up Amazon S3 lifecycle rules?” with results limited to aws.amazon.com and docs.aws.amazon.com.

Figure 4: A test search with included domains

  • Integrate. When the results look right, you have two options: Generate code snippet: get code that calls the API with the same settings, ready to paste into your agent or application. Create gateway target: add Web Search as a tool on an AgentCore Gateway, so agents can call it through MCP.

The console signs each call with your own IAM identity, so your role needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch permission.

When to use the API compared to the gateway

ScenarioRecommended path
Building agents with MCP-compatible toolsAgentCore Gateway
Several tools behind one MCP endpoint, with optional MCP sessionsAgentCore Gateway
One administrator source policy for many agents and teamsAgentCore Gateway
MCP clients that need search, such as Claude with the AWS Web Search connectorAgentCore Gateway
Custom orchestrationWeb Search API
Non-agent use cases (dashboards, pipelines)Web Search API
Want direct control over retries and cachingWeb Search API
Adding web search to an existing applicationWeb Search API

Both paths search the same index. They differ in a few ways. A gateway can also authorize callers with a JSON Web Token (JWT), while the API authorizes with IAM only. On a gateway, an administrator can set domain lists on the target that apply to every request without the calling agent seeing them. With the API, each request carries its own filters. The field names differ too: the API takes searchQuery, publishedAfter, and publishedBefore, and the gateway’s MCP tool takes query, from, and to. For more guidance, see Choose between the API and the Gateway connector.

Pricing

The Web Search API meters to the same usage type as the gateway connector, so it’s billed at the Web Search rate of $7 per 1,000 queries. Because no gateway is involved, there are no gateway charges. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

Availability

The Web Search API is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions. For the current list, see Supported AWS Regions.

Get started

Use the following resources to help you get started.

  • Web Search API documentation
  • Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
  • InvokeWebSearch API reference

About the authors

item.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026

At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands, our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production.

As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume.

What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents.

Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock

Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable.

Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode.

Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation.

Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline.

Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI, a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty.

Build and run agents you can rely on

Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0. We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations.

Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback. Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority. Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client.

Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows, including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps.

Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model.

Keep answers grounded in sources you trust. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location for requests made with the OpenAI Responses API. You can allow up to 100 domains, block up to 100 domains, and return results relevant to a geography. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then checks that answers stay true to their sources. Its new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks costs the same as the Classic tier, covers conversational and reasoning responses, and supports more languages. With both, you can control where answers come from and catch hallucinations in more of your applications.

Predict and lower the cost of running agents

Pay for agent memory based on what you use. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now prices short-term memory by the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, instead of a flat rate per event. Most workloads see lower costs, and small-payload use cases see the largest reductions. You can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records to meet retention requirements and control storage costs.

See what drives your Amazon Bedrock spend. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now break down Amazon Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature, at no additional charge. Finance and platform teams can find their most expensive models or set a budget alert for a single model, in the billing tools they already use. To lower input costs, Advanced Prompt Optimization can now also shorten your prompts, returning a shorter version only when it scores at least as high on your evaluation.

Build voice, local, and well-tested agents with Strands

Ship voice agents in a few lines of code. Strands Bidi Agents, for building two-way, speech-to-speech voice agents, are now generally available, with direct support for Amazon Nova Sonic, OpenAI, and Gemini models. Bidi Agents reconnect to the model in the background, so long calls keep going past a provider’s session limit. A voice agent can also hand longer work, such as research, to another agent and explain the results aloud.

Let local agents work within your limits. Strands Box, now in developer preview, is an open source local sandbox for AI agents. It combines operating-system isolation with semantic policy. You set policy for each tool, and Box enforces it deterministically, whether the agent calls tools directly, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or by generating code. Box works with any model and any agent framework, so an agent can operate in your project without reaching files and services you didn’t allow.

Find where your agent breaks before customers do. Red teaming in Strands Evals runs adversarial conversations, such as prompt injections and jailbreak attempts, against your agent and shows the messages and tool calls where it failed. Strands Evals can now also score structured output field by field, giving partial credit when an agent gets most fields right. Use them to fix weak spots before an agent reaches production. To get started, see the Strands Evals documentation.

Cut the cost of routine agent decisions. Strands Decider, the small, open source decision model we featured in last month’s recap, now comes in four sizes built on Gemma 4. Instead of generating text, it picks between options you define, such as which tool to call or where to route a request. When an Amazon team switched ticket classification in one of its largest internal ticketing systems to Decider, estimated cost per ticket dropped by about 98 percent. Average response time dropped by 78 percent.

Get started

Explore Amazon Bedrock, deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI, or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK.

Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation.

About the author

item.title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track

From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent. At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play.

There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live.

The basics: Session types

If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics.

re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel, while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions.
