The pipeline picks up metadata files, generates vector embeddings with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and indexes them into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Once indexed, the table is discoverable by all connected agents without manual re-indexing or server restarts.

To improve accuracy for specific applications, an engineer can optionally associate the dataset with a business context. This narrows the search scope, so the agent prioritizes the right tables. The following example shows a context mapping entry:

{
  "delivery_metrics": {
    "description": "Delivery accuracy and defect attribution data",
    "tables": ["analytics_db.customer_orders_summary"],
    "sources": {"wiki": [], "quip": []}
  }
}

If no context is specified, the agent searches across all indexed tables. The context mapping reduces latency and improves SQL accuracy by limiting the search space. This scoping is optional and can be added at any time without modifying the metadata files themselves.

Putting it together: A query in action

When a user asks, “What were our top 10 highest-value orders last month?”, the client enriches the request with business context to narrow scope. The agent converts the question into a vector embedding, searches the metadata catalog for matching schemas, and selects the most relevant table via a lightweight LLM call.

Using the selected schema, column descriptions, and engine-specific query hints, the agent generates a SQL statement such as:

SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount, order_date
FROM analytics_db.regional_order_summary
WHERE order_date >= date_add('month', -1, current_date)
ORDER BY total_amount DESC
LIMIT 10

The SQL is validated and auto-corrected for engine compatibility, then executed against Amazon Athena. The agent formats the results into a natural language response and streams it back to the user. In our testing, this end-to-end flow completes within 15–20 seconds.

The same orchestration extends beyond pure SQL. Because document search is registered as another tool on the same server, the agent can answer questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single turn, such as “What was our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” For that request, the agent runs an Athena query for the return-rate figure and a Knowledge Bases document search for the analysis, then combines both into one response.

Security and multi-tenant access

That single-turn orchestration works only because every tool call passes through the same controlled gateway. The architecture uses layered security rather than a single enforcement point. The MCP server runs in private subnets behind an internal Application Load Balancer and is not reachable from the internet. Only the client layer, which sits behind a public-facing Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF, can route requests to it. Amazon Cognito validates user identity at the client layer, and only authenticated, token-bearing requests are forwarded downstream. At the tool level, the Athena query tools enforce SELECT-only queries, rejecting write operations before they reach the data lake. All tool invocations are logged to Amazon CloudWatch with structured JSON, which gives security teams a single audit point for data access across every agent and application. This architecture is available in the AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases are available.

This centralized design is also what makes the server multi-tenant. Because the standardized /mcp endpoint accepts any MCP-compatible client regardless of which LLM or orchestration framework it uses, multiple agents share the same tools and the same access controls. Adding a new agent requires only pointing it at the server endpoint, so onboarding another team extends the system without weakening or duplicating the security model.

Serverless infrastructure and scaling

Each layer scales through a mechanism suited to its workload pattern:

LayerScaling mechanismTrigger
Client (ECS Fargate)ECS Service Auto ScalingCPU utilization (50% threshold)
MCP Server (ECS Fargate)ECS Service Auto ScalingCPU/Memory utilization
AthenaServerless (automatic)Query concurrency
Amazon BedrockManaged service scalingInference requests

Amazon ECS Fargate provides serverless compute with no EC2 instances to manage. Downstream services (Athena, Bedrock) scale automatically, so the system handles a single query or hundreds of concurrent queries without configuration changes.

Use cases and extensions

This architecture supports several patterns beyond basic question-answering. Enterprise knowledge assistants can combine data lake queries with document search to answer complex questions spanning both structured data and unstructured knowledge, such as “What’s our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” Internal analytics copilots let business users query the data lake conversationally without writing SQL, relying on the metadata descriptions and query hints to guide the agent toward accurate, performant query patterns.

The standardized /mcp endpoint also supports multi-agent workflows. Multiple specialized agents for data analysis, document retrieval, and operational alerting can share the same MCP server, each accessing the full tool suite through a common protocol. Onboarding a new team’s data follows the same configuration-driven pattern. They add a metadata JSON file, and within one pipeline sync cycle their dataset is discoverable by every connected agent and application.

Conclusion

A centralized MCP server on Amazon ECS Fargate provides a scalable, secure gateway between AI agents and enterprise data lakes. The metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and the Model Context Protocol standard means any MCP-compatible client can connect without custom adapters.

The key architectural decision is separating the tool layer from the agent layer. Agents evolve rapidly, but data access patterns should outlive any single agent implementation. Treating extensibility as a configuration problem rather than a code problem accelerates onboarding.

To learn more, see Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases user guide, Amazon Athena, and the Model Context Protocol specification.

Next steps

We are extending this architecture in two directions. First, finer-grained access control where table owners can mark sensitive columns as restricted per permission group, and the agent automatically excludes those columns from generated SQL without prompt-level changes.

Second, closing the feedback loop so that when queries fail or produce low-confidence results, the system captures the failure pattern and surfaces targeted suggestions for improving column descriptions, adding query hints.

About the authors

item.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon…
item.description: Full title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2

In Part 1, you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server.

The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools:

What Part 1 doesWhy it stops scalingWhat Part 2 does instead
The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directlyN agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs itAgents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry
The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secretEvery agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reachThe Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions
Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own codeThe same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one placeOne default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run

In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant.

What changes from Part 1

The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions.

Figure 1: The Part 1 solution with AgentCore Gateway, Policy, and Observability, a second agent on Amazon EKS, and the audit path, with numbers matching the steps that follow

  • The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1.
  • The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG.
  • Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs.
  • Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target.
  • For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG.
  • The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an authz.check span.
  • Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.

The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway.

Prerequisites

In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following:

PrerequisiteNeeded for
eksctl, kubectl, and DockerThe second agent on Amazon EKS
Okta Log StreamingOkta’s System Log in CloudWatch
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissionsAgentCore Gateways and policy engines, Amazon EKS clusters, CloudWatch log groups, and Amazon EventBridge rules

The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.

Create a Gateway that accepts the ID-JAG

The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent:

authorizer = {"customJWTAuthorizer": {
    "discoveryUrl": f"{OKTA_ORG}/.well-known/openid-configuration",  # the ID-JAG's issuer
    "allowedAudience": [f"{OKTA_ORG}/oauth2/{CUSTOM_AS_ID}"],         # the resource's authorization server
    "allowedClients": [AGENT_CLIENT_ID],                               # only this agent's ID-JAGs
    "allowedScopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"],
}}

Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer.

Figure 2: The Gateway accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to the agent for the resource’s authorization server

Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange:

"credentialProviderConfigurations": [{
    "credentialProviderType": "OAUTH",
    "credentialProvider": {"oauthCredentialProvider": {
        "providerArn": provider_arn,          # the JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT provider from Part 1
        "scopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"],  # must equal the ID-JAG's scopes
        "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    }},
}]

Figure 3 shows a target configured this way.

Figure 3: The task manager target redeems the ID-JAG through the Part 1 credential provider

Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema (listingMode set to DEFAULT with an inline mcpToolSchema), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages tools/list by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life.

Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself.

Bind tools to agents with Cedar

Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in ENFORCE mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped permit grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped forbid blocks nothing. Guard each tag with hasTag:

permit(
  principal is AgentCore::OAuthUser,
  action in [AgentCore::Action::"taskmanager___create_task",
             AgentCore::Action::"taskmanager___update_task_status"],
  resource == AgentCore::Gateway::"<gateway-arn>"
) when {
  principal.hasTag("client_id") && principal.getTag("client_id") == "<agent-client-id>" &&
  principal.hasTag("scope") &&
  (principal.getTag("scope") == "xaa:write" ||
   principal.getTag("scope") like "xaa:write *" ||
   principal.getTag("scope") like "* xaa:write" ||
   principal.getTag("scope") like "* xaa:write *")
};

The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated scope claim, so the four conditions match xaa:write only as a whole entry. A scope such as xaa:write-admin doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with xaa:read. Check that every policy is ACTIVE before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the groups claim, as in Part 1.

Point the agent at the Gateway

Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself:

id_jag = context.request_headers["Authorization"].removeprefix("Bearer ")  # allowlisted header
tools = make_client(GATEWAY_URL, id_jag)  # the Gateway redeems the ID-JAG for each target

Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep allowedClients on the runtime’s authorizer.

Run a second agent on Amazon EKS

Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only xaa:read, and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup.

Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type oauth-id-jag+jwt, expiry, and that client_id is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to REGISTERED_AGENTS. Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to localhost unless you set DOCKER_CONTAINER=true.

Trace every decision with AgentCore Observability

The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability, the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as traces.default, which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events.

One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision:

SpanEmitted byWhat it records
AgentCore.Gateway.InboundAuthGatewayWhether the inbound ID-JAG was issued to this agent
AgentCore.Policy.AuthorizeActionPolicyThe Cedar decision for this tool
AgentCore.Identity.GetWorkloadAccessTokenIdentityBinding the agent’s workload identity to the user
AgentCore.Identity.GetResourceOauth2TokenIdentityRedeeming the ID-JAG at Okta for a scoped access token
AgentCore.Gateway.InvokeToolGatewayThe tool call and its outcome
authz.checkThe MCP server (ADOT)The user’s groups, the agent, the decision, and the reason

Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni.

Figure 4: The audit path, where spans and Okta’s System Log reach CloudWatch and one Omni query joins them

To set it up:

  • Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search, turn on trace delivery for each Gateway (see this sample script), and add ADOT to the BFF and the MCP servers. The task manager writes each decision, the user, and the agent onto an authz.check span.
  • In Okta, add a Log Stream for Amazon EventBridge. Okta delivers each event to a partner event bus in your account, and a rule writes it to a CloudWatch Logs log group. In our tests, events arrived about 1 second after Okta published them. Each ID-JAG grant event names the agent as the actor, the user as a target, and the granted scopes and resource connection.
  • Set up an Omni space in the account and AWS Region, add the Okta log group to the CloudWatch Dataset integration, and save a view, view.xaa_authz_decisions, over the authz.check spans.

One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to:

SELECT o.okta_time, o.agent, o.user_email, o.granted, a.decision_time, a.decision, a.reason
FROM (SELECT `@timestamp` AS okta_time, detail['actor']['id'] AS agent_id,
             detail['actor']['displayName'] AS agent,
             array_element(regexp_match(`@message`, '"type"\s*:\s*"User"\s*,\s*"alternateId"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"'), 1) AS user_email,
             detail['debugContext']['debugData']['grantedScopes'] AS granted
      FROM "logs.default"
      WHERE `@timestamp` BETWEEN NOW() - INTERVAL '1' HOUR AND NOW()
        AND detail['eventType'] = 'app.oauth2.token.grant.id_jag') o
JOIN (SELECT `@timestamp` AS decision_time, user_id, agent_client_id, decision, reason
      FROM "view.xaa_authz_decisions"
      WHERE `@timestamp` BETWEEN NOW() - INTERVAL '1' HOUR AND NOW()) a
  ON a.user_id = o.user_email AND a.agent_client_id = o.agent_id
 AND a.decision_time BETWEEN o.okta_time AND o.okta_time + INTERVAL '5' MINUTE

For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent xaa:read xaa:write for her, then the MCP server denying her create_task 16.7 seconds later and allowing list_tasks after that, as Figure 5 shows.

Figure 5: The Omni query joins Alice’s ID-JAG grant in Okta’s System Log to the two decisions it led to

Each request is also one trace, from the BFF through the agent, the Gateway’s identity and policy checks, and the MCP server’s decision, as Figure 6 shows. Omni marks the trace as a fault because the agent’s create_task call returned the denial.

Figure 6: One trace for Alice’s request, from the agent’s tool call through the Gateway’s identity and Cedar checks to the MCP server’s deny

Two instrumentation details matter. ADOT finds the Region and signs its exports through botocore, so add botocore to services that lack it. Until we did, our MCP servers exported no spans. And ADOT’s agent mode turns off instrumentation for HTTP client libraries such as requests and urllib3 by default, so set OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS in your BFF to override that default with a list that leaves out the BFF’s HTTP client (requests, in ours), or its trace context won’t reach the agent.

Validate the results

We ran each check through both Gateways with the users from Part 1. Each session listed the tools, then called list_tasks, create_task, and an employee lookup:

Caller and pathTools listedcreate_taskReads
Alice, agent A, Gateway A6Denied by the MCP server: requires xaa-writersAllowed
Bob, agent A, Gateway A6CreatedAllowed
Carol, agent A, Gateway A6Denied by the MCP server: no groups claimAllowed
Bob, agent B, Gateway B4: Cedar hid the write toolsRefused by the Gateway: “No policy applies to the request (denied by default)”Allowed

Through the deployed agents, the results matched: agent A denied Alice and Carol and created Bob’s task, and agent B told Bob it had no tool to create tasks. The same user got different authority through different agents, and Okta decided it.

These requests stopped at the front door:

RequestResponse
Agent B’s ID-JAG at Gateway A, or agent A’s at Gateway BHTTP 403, MCP error -32002 insufficient_scope
An Okta access token instead of an ID-JAGHTTP 403, the same error
No tokenHTTP 401, “Missing Bearer token”
Agent A’s ID-JAG sent to agent B on EKSRefused in 98 milliseconds, before a model call: “issued to a different agent”

The Gateway returns the same generic error for a wrong agent and for the wrong token type, so check your configuration against the token’s client_id and aud when you see it.

The Gateway’s identity and policy work is small next to the tool itself. Medians and 90th percentiles from 24 hours of Gateway A spans in Omni:

Spanp50p90
Gateway.InboundAuth34 ms69 ms
Identity.Authorize25 ms60 ms
Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken48 ms94 ms
Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token70 ms439 ms
Policy.AuthorizeAction (Cedar, per call)47 ms56 ms
Policy.PartiallyAuthorizeActions (Cedar, per tool listing)65 ms75 ms
Gateway.TargetInvocation (the MCP server on AgentCore runtime)5,565 ms6,273 ms

The identity and policy spans for one tool call sum to about 0.2 seconds at their medians, and the MCP server’s own authz.check span took under 1 millisecond. Gateway B showed the same pattern, with GetResourceOauth2Token at 408 milliseconds at the median.

Cross App Access or per-user consent

XAA applies where the target application’s authorization server accepts an ID-JAG. There, your Okta administrator decides which agent may act for which users, users see no consent prompt, and Okta evaluates policy each time a token is requested. Applications with their own authorization servers, such as GitHub, rely on each user’s own OAuth consent instead. Figure 7 compares the two, as we measured them.

Figure 7: Cross App Access compared with per-user OAuth consent, with the revocation behavior we measured

We deployed the AWS sample 07-consent-portal-auth-code-flow-targets beside our stack, with Okta signing users in to an AgentCore Identity consent portal and a GitHub target on its own Gateway. Alice connected a GitHub test account through the portal, and Bob never connected one. The post Manage end-user OAuth consent for AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore describes this lane in full. Here’s what we observed:

ActionNext GitHub tool call
Alice consented in the portalReturned her GitHub identity
Bob, who never consentedMCP error -32042 with an AgentCore authorization URL
Alice suspended in Okta, earlier token reusedStill worked: the Gateway checks the inbound token’s signature and expiry, and that token lived 1 hour
Alice suspended, new sign-inRefused
Alice unsuspendedWorked with no new consent
Alice’s grant disconnected through the consent portal’s APINot connected, then -32042 again

The two lanes revoke differently. In XAA, Okta’s controls stop the next ID-JAG mint, and issued tokens expire within about 5 minutes. In the consent lane, Okta controls only sign-in: the stored grant outlived the suspension and stayed until we disconnected it. Choose per target application, not once for the enterprise.

Where this pattern applies

In media and entertainment, the fleet arrives quickly. A studio or streaming or games organization has agents for production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support, each sitting in front of a different system with its own authorization model and its own auditors. The question isn’t whether one agent can be governed. It’s whether the hundredth one is governed the same way, and whether an administrator can still answer which agents reach which systems for which users.

Nothing here is specific to that industry. The agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the Gateway is where authorization is decided. Teams in financial services, healthcare, and the public sector put different resources behind the same front door and get the same audit trail.

What’s next: observability and evaluations

This post uses AgentCore Observability for one purpose: to prove that each allow and deny traces back to a control. There’s more in it than that, and it’s a body of work in its own right. The spans already carry the model and tool latency behind every governance decision, Transaction Search can alert on a spike in denials, and AgentCore evaluations can score an agent’s behavior against your own criteria, online for live traffic or on demand over a chosen set of spans. A later post takes that up: what to measure on a governed agent, which evaluators catch an agent that reports success after a refused tool call, and how to run both without turning your traces into your largest bill.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the Part 2 resources, then follow the cleanup steps in Part 1:

  • Delete the Amazon EKS cluster (eksctl delete cluster) and its Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
  • Delete the Gateways and their targets, then the Policy in AgentCore engines, and then agent B’s credential provider.
  • Delete the CloudWatch Omni space and domain, the Dataset integration, the Amazon EventBridge rule and partner event bus, and the CloudWatch log groups.
  • If you deployed sample 07, follow its cleanup steps.
  • Delete the IAM roles and policies you created.
  • In Okta, delete the log stream, and deactivate and delete agent B and its linked app.

Conclusion

In this post, you moved the Part 1 solution from a topology that suits a few agents and tools to one that holds up across many. The Gateway became the single front door and redeemed Okta’s grant, so the agents held no tool credentials. Cedar policies evaluated by Policy in AgentCore replaced the check copied into each server. A second agent on Amazon EKS joined under its own Okta identity. And AgentCore Observability, with Okta’s System Log beside it in CloudWatch Omni, traced each allow and deny back to the agent, the user, and the control that decided it. The governance mechanism didn’t change, which is the point: only the topology around it did.

To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For plain token exchange through a Gateway, read Implement on-behalf-of token exchange for multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

About the authors

item.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon…
item.description: Full title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1

An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end.

In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch.

Solution overview

Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime.

Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow

Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this:

  • The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app.
  • For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  • The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent.
  • The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens.
  • The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups.
  • The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool.

Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes.

Figure 2: The three-token chain and the check each party makes, with the step 4 workload access token staying inside AWS

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need the following:

PrerequisiteWhat we used
An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon BedrockUS West (Oregon)
An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers)An Okta Integrator Free Plan org
Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCorePython 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissionsPermission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles

The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.

Register the agent in Okta

Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.

  • Create a custom authorization server for the resource application with the audience api://task-manager and the custom scopes xaa:read and xaa:write. Request only the resource’s custom scopes: Okta rejects an ID-JAG request that includes OpenID Connect scopes such as openid or profile (invalid_scope), so a request needs at least one custom scope and no OpenID Connect scopes.
  • Add a groups claim to its access tokens, filtered to groups that start with xaa-. This claim carries each user’s authority to the tools.
  • In the Admin Console, go to Directory > AI Agents, choose Register AI agent and then Register manually, optionally assign an owner, and create a linked OpenID Connect app. On Client registration, choose Client secret, generate a secret, and then activate the agent. The agent and the app share one client ID, and that app must sign your users in: an ID token from another app fails the exchange with “the client application is not registered for delegation to this agent.”
  • On the agent’s Resource connections tab, connect it to the authorization server, limited to the scopes it needs, as Figure 3 shows.
  • Add an access policy rule to the custom authorization server that allows the agent’s JWT Bearer grant, with a 5-minute access token lifetime. Without the grant type, the second exchange fails with no_matching_policy, and the lifetime bounds how long a revoked delegation keeps working.
  • Assign the users or groups who might act through the agent. They sign in through the linked app, so give it an app sign-in policy that admits them with the authenticators they’ve enrolled. In our sandbox org, the linked app had its own policy with a rule for the test group. For real users, apply your organization’s policy, including multifactor authentication.

Figure 3: The task agent’s resource connection in Okta, limited to the xaa:read and xaa:write scopes

Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent:

POST /oauth2/v1/token HTTP/1.1
Host: YOUR-ORG.okta.com
Authorization: Basic <the agent's client ID and secret>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&subject_token=<the user's ID token>
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&audience=https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/oauth2/YOUR-CUSTOM-AS-ID
&scope=xaa:read xaa:write

The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python (agent/xaa_client.py). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files.

Set up AgentCore Identity

AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint:

Part of AgentCore IdentityWhat it holdsWho creates it
Workload identityThe agent’s identity on AWS, bound to the signed-in user for each requestAgentCore runtime, for each agent runtime
OAuth2 credential providerThe agent’s Okta client ID and secret, and the grant to useYou, once per Okta agent
Token vaultThe access tokens the provider obtainsAgentCore Identity

Create the credential provider

The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT, which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion:

control = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control")
provider = control.create_oauth2_credential_provider(
    name="okta-xaa-obo",
    credentialProviderVendor="CustomOauth2",
    oauth2ProviderConfigInput={"customOauth2ProviderConfig": {
        "oauthDiscovery": {"discoveryUrl": f"{OKTA_ORG}/oauth2/{CUSTOM_AS_ID}/.well-known/openid-configuration"},
        "clientId": AGENT_CLIENT_ID,          # the AI agent's Okta client ID
        "clientSecret": AGENT_CLIENT_SECRET,  # AgentCore Identity stores it in AWS Secrets Manager
        "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC",
        "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": {"grantType": "JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT"},
    }},
)
provider_arn = provider["credentialProviderArn"]

Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider. If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console.

Figure 4: The credential provider authenticating as the agent with the JWT authorization grant

Use the workload identity that AgentCore runtime manages

AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange.

The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext, not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead:

from bedrock_agentcore.runtime import BedrockAgentCoreContext

identity = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore")

def okta_access_token() -> str:
    workload_token = BedrockAgentCoreContext.get_workload_access_token()  # minted by the runtime
    return identity.get_resource_oauth2_token(
        workloadIdentityToken=workload_token,
        resourceCredentialProviderName="okta-xaa-obo",
        scopes=["xaa:read", "xaa:write"],  # must equal the ID-JAG's scopes
        oauth2Flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    )["accessToken"]

AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way (agent/agent.py).

Scope the agent’s role to its workload identity and provider

AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret:

[
  {
    "Sid": "OktaOnBehalfOf",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:GetResourceOauth2Token",
    "Resource": [
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default/workload-identity/RUNTIME-WORKLOAD-IDENTITY",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/okta-xaa-obo"
    ]
  },
  {
    "Sid": "ReadProviderSecret",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:123456789012:secret:bedrock-agentcore-identity!default/oauth2/okta-xaa-obo-*"
  }
]

Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime, and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn: the segment is oauth2credentialprovider, and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException. The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements.

Deploy the agent on AgentCore runtime

Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.json:

"authorizerType": "CUSTOM_JWT",
"authorizerConfiguration": {
  "customJwtAuthorizer": {
    "discoveryUrl": "https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration",
    "allowedAudience": ["https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/oauth2/YOUR-CUSTOM-AS-ID"],
    "allowedClients": ["YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"],
    "allowedScopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"]
  }
}

allowedClients matches the client_id claim that an ID-JAG carries. Without it, the runtime admitted another agent’s ID-JAG with HTTP 200 and the request failed later, at the exchange. With it, the runtime refused that token with HTTP 401.

Besides the policy from the previous section, the execution role needs bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream. It needs no bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime permission for the MCP servers: each runs on AgentCore runtime behind its own JWT authorizer, with the custom authorization server as issuer and api://task-manager as audience, so the agent calls it with the Okta access token as a bearer token, not with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).

Enforce each user’s authority in the MCP server

The resource connection sets the scopes for every user of an agent, so all three test users received xaa:read xaa:write, and per-user authority travels in the groups claim instead: Alice’s token carried xaa-readers, Bob’s xaa-writers, and Carol’s had none.

The task manager checks two things: it accepts only tokens a registered agent obtained, and it allows a write only when the group and the scope are both present:

REGISTERED_AGENTS = {"YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"}

def _require_agent() -> None:
    claims = _decode_claims()  # the runtime's JWT authorizer already validated the token
    agent = (claims.get("act") or {}).get("sub")
    if agent in REGISTERED_AGENTS and claims.get("cid") == agent:
        return
    raise ToolError("insufficient_privileges: this server accepts only tokens that a registered "
                    "AI agent obtained through Okta Cross App Access")

def _require_write() -> None:
    _require_agent()
    if WRITERS_GROUP in _groups() and "xaa:write" in _scopes():
        return
    raise ToolError(f"insufficient_privileges: this tool requires membership in '{WRITERS_GROUP}'")

Both checks close gaps we found: a write check that allowed tokens without a groups claim let Carol, who belongs to neither group, create tasks, and before _require_agent a plain token-exchange token, issued to a service app with no act claim, created a task for Bob. The server can read the claims without verifying the token again only because the runtime’s JWT authorizer already verified it. A server without that authorizer in front of it must check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry itself, as the Part 2 agent on Amazon EKS does.

Validate the results

We ran every check against the deployed solution. Alice, Bob, and Carol each asked the agent to create a task and then list the project’s tasks:

Callercreate_tasklist_tasks
AliceDenied: requires membership in xaa-writersAllowed
BobCreatedAllowed
CarolDenied: no groups claimAllowed
Bob, then Alice right after himCreated for Bob, then denied for Alice: no authority carried overAllowed

These requests stopped before tools ran:

RequestStopped byResponse
Agent B’s ID-JAG sent to the task agentThe runtime’s JWT authorizer401: “Claim ‘client_id’ value mismatch with configuration.”
An ID-JAG held for 245 secondsThe runtime’s JWT authorizer401: “Ineffectual token, will expire within the next minute”
A malformed bearer tokenThe runtime’s JWT authorizer403: “Failed to parse token”
One ID-JAG redeemed twiceOkta’s custom authorization server400: “The id-jag was already used.”
A narrower scope at the second exchangeOkta’s custom authorization server400: “The scope parameter must exactly match the scopes in the id-jag.”
A scope outside the connectionOkta’s org authorization server400 invalid_scope
A plain token exchange token at the MCP serverThe MCP serverDenied: only tokens that a registered AI agent obtained

The token that AgentCore Identity returned matched one we redeemed directly at Okta, claim for claim: sub was the user, cid and act named the agent, scp held the connection’s scopes, groups held the user’s groups, and it lived 300 seconds.

AgentCore Identity adds about 0.6 seconds to a request that takes about 30 seconds end to end, most of it model and tool calls. Medians of five runs from our test client:

CallMedian
Sign-in, scripted (authorization code flow)1,205 ms
ID token to ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server216 ms
GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT135 ms
GetResourceOauth2Token, including Okta’s JWT bearer grant508 ms

Govern agents in operation

Okta evaluates the agent, the user, and the connection when it mints an ID-JAG. We measured what each administrator action does to the next request and to issued tokens:

Admin action in OktaNew requestsTokens already issued
Delete the agent’s resource connectionRefused immediately (invalid_target)Work until they expire, up to 5 minutes
Remove the user’s assignmentRefused within about 1 second, even with an ID token the user already heldUp to 5 minutes
Deactivate the agentRefused after Okta runs the operation, which our test org queued for 86 minutesUp to 5 minutes

Actions on one agent left the other working. Okta doesn’t re-check the user when an ID-JAG is redeemed: its custom authorization server issued an access token 3 seconds after we removed a user, for an ID-JAG minted before the removal. Okta’s System Log records each grant with the agent as the actor, and Part 2 streams those events into CloudWatch.

Best practices for the delegation chain

Six practices came out of these measurements, each one a property of the chain rather than a preference:

PracticeWhat we measured
Mint a fresh ID-JAG for each requestAn ID-JAG is single-use and lives 300 seconds. The runtime refuses one with under 60 seconds left, so 225 seconds worked, 245 didn’t
Carry per-user authority in the groups claim, and request one scope set per requestOkta sets scopes from the resource connection, so all three users got the same scopes, and the second exchange must request exactly the ID-JAG’s
Pin the agent at the runtime, and check act and cid in the toolallowedClients matches the client_id claim an ID-JAG carries. Okta access tokens carry cid instead
Reproduce a failed exchange directly against OktaThrough AgentCore Identity, a scope mismatch and a wrong client both surface as “Token exchange failed with HTTP status 400”
Grant the agent’s role read access to the provider’s secretGetResourceOauth2Token failed until the role could read it
Keep lifetimes short, and use the resource connection as your kill switchDeleting the connection took effect immediately. Deactivating the agent sat in Okta’s beta AI agent API queue for 86 minutes, with no cancel

Cross App Access compared with plain token exchange

Plain RFC 8693 token exchange also carries the user’s identity downstream. We compared it with XAA against the same Okta authorization server and user:

Behavior we observedPlain token exchangeCross App Access
Agent identity in the tokenNo act claimact names the agent
ScopesWidened: Alice’s own token had xaa:read, and the exchange returned xaa:read xaa:writeThe scopes the administrator approved
Exchange rule limited to xaa-writersAlice still received a tokenAlice denied
User unassigned, earlier token reusedStill exchangedRefused
What administrators seeA service app with a grant typeThe agent, its connections, and the agent in each log event

These results reflect our Okta configuration. Okta’s guide shows an act claim for exchanged tokens, which we didn’t receive. Plain token exchange carried the user’s identity, but not the user’s authority.

Where this pattern applies

We work with media and entertainment companies, and this is where we met the problem first. A studio or streaming or games organization runs agents against production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support. Each system has its own authorization model and its own auditors, and a user’s authority differs by title, territory, or release window, so “which agent might act for which user in which system” has to be answered before an agent ships.

Nothing in the chain is specific to that industry: the agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the user’s authority rides in a claim. Financial services, healthcare, and public sector teams put different resources behind the same controls.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:

  • Delete the AWS CloudFormation stacks that the AgentCore CLI created for the agent and the two MCP servers.
  • Delete the credential provider with aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name okta-xaa-obo, and any workload identity you created yourself with delete-workload-identity.
  • Delete the IAM policies you added to the execution roles.
  • In Okta, deactivate and delete the AI agent and its linked app, and remove the resource connection, the authorization server’s policy rule, scopes, and claim, and the test users and groups.

Conclusion

In this post, you used Okta Cross App Access to decide which agent might act for which user, and AgentCore Identity to carry out each decision. The runtime admitted only the agent’s own ID-JAGs, the credential provider redeemed each one with a secret the agent didn’t hold, the token vault reused the result within a request, and the MCP server enforced each user’s authority from the groups claim.

This design keeps the exchange in the agent’s role and repeats the authorization check in every MCP server. See Part 2 of this series to learn why its design moves both behind one AgentCore Gateway with Cedar policies, adds a second agent on Amazon EKS, and joins the Okta System Log with AgentCore traces in CloudWatch.

To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For the API details, see On-behalf-of token exchange in the AgentCore Developer Guide.

About the authors

item.title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on…
item.description: Full title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds.

This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries.

What Greenlight needed to solve

Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks.

Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors:

  • Dark web breach cards – Card Network and internal threat intel flag Greenlight customer cards found on the dark web.
  • Identity and access anomalies – Unusual login patterns, privilege escalations, and policy violations across Identity Provider (IdP) and internal systems.
  • Infrastructure alerts – Signals from Signals from EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), Asset Inventory, and other observability tools.
  • Financial risk events – Suspicious transaction patterns, compliance triggers, and fraud indicators from card processing systems.

Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks.

Greenlight needed a system that could:

  • Triage and resolve routine cases autonomously at machine speed.
  • Escalate complex cases with full context to human analysts.
  • Learn from resolution patterns to improve accuracy over time.
  • Operate within financial services compliance guardrails.

Architecture: Tiered multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity.

Figure 1: Luna’s tiered supervisor architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Tier 1 supervisor: High-volume triage

Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents:

DomainWhat the agent does
Identity and AccessChecks login history, MFA status, session anomalies
Endpoint DetectionPulls endpoint alerts, process trees, IOC matches
ObservabilityCorrelates infrastructure metrics with alert timing
Asset InventoryMaps affected assets, ownership, exposure surface
Data AnalyticsQueries historical patterns and baseline deviations
Payment ProcessingVerifies card status, transaction history, account state
Customer ExperienceReviews customer session behavior around incident time
Customer SupportChecks related open tickets, prior complaints
Code and RepositoriesTraces code changes correlated with alerts
Project TrackingLinks incidents to recent deployments or known issues
Threat IntelligenceEnriches IOCs with external threat context
Automation (SOAR)Executes approved remediation playbooks

The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds.

Tier 2 supervisor: Deep-dive investigation

Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning:

  • Re-investigates escalated cases with deeper cross-source correlation.
  • Invokes specialized agents through boto3 with expanded context windows.
  • Chains reasoning across 3–5 data sources to establish causality.
  • Produces detailed investigation reports with evidence chains for human review.

The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases.

Entry points for different personas

Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives:

  • Tines SOAR – Primary volume driver. Automated alert ingestion feeds cases directly into Tier 1.
  • Security, Risk, and ProdOps engineers – Direct API access for ad-hoc investigation requests.
  • Claude Desktop extension – Chat-based interface for on-call engineers. An engineer opens the extension, describes what they want investigated, and Luna executes a deep-dive with full tool access.

Memory and learning: How Luna gets smarter over time

The memory layer is built on AgentCore memory. This layer is what separates Luna from a stateless triage tool. It supports pattern recognition, deduplication, and continuous accuracy improvement.

Episodic memory (30-day rolling window)

Stores recent events and resolution outcomes. When a new alert arrives, Luna checks: “Have I seen this pattern in the last 30 days? What was the verdict? Is this a known behavior that I should allowlist?”

Concrete example: A Greenlight infrastructure role generates a specific access pattern every Tuesday at 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. Without memory, Luna would flag this every week. With episodic memory, Luna learned after the first resolution that this pattern is expected and auto-allowlists it.

Long-term memory

Persists semantic preferences and resolution templates beyond the 30-day window:

  • “This access pattern is expected because that’s the role’s purpose.”
  • Greenlight’s historical case data shows “Cards from this specific dark web source have a 73 percent false-positive rate – prioritize deduplication.”
  • Resolution templates for recurring case types that encode institutional knowledge.

Case-learnings pipeline

A dedicated pipeline feeds resolution outcomes back into the system:

  • Ingestion – An AWS Lambda function captures every case resolution from Tines events.
  • Learnings + Dedup – DynamoDB stores resolution patterns and deduplicates similar cases. When Luna resolves a case the same way three times, it records that as a confirmed pattern.
  • Digest – A Lambda function processes new learnings into actionable context that supervisors consume at inference time.
  • Feedback loop – Resolution learnings feed back into Tier 1, improving first-pass accuracy incrementally.

This pipeline drove Luna’s autonomous resolution rate from 83 percent (Tier 1 only) to more than 90 percent (Tier 1, Tier 2, and learnings).

Expanding from SOC into financial risk triage

Greenlight expanded Luna into financial risk assessment within two months of the SOC deployment. The architectural changes were minimal: new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor layered onto the existing infrastructure.

Dark web breach card workflow

When a Greenlight customer card appears on the dark web, Luna executes this workflow autonomously:

  • Ingest – Threat intel providers (Mastercard, internal feeds) report compromised card numbers.
  • Verify – Luna queries Galileo: Does this card belong to Greenlight? Is it currently active? What’s the recent transaction history?
  • Deduplicate – DynamoDB check: Is this a repeat notification? Has this card already been remediated? Multiple providers often report the same breach.
  • Cross-reference – Query Mixpanel for customer session anomalies, Zendesk for related tickets, and internal fraud scoring.
  • Assess and act – Determine risk levels. Low risk: log and monitor. Medium risk: flag for review. High risk: escalate to human analysts with full evidence chain.

Greenlight receives hundreds of breach card notifications daily. Luna processes each in seconds. A human analyst doing the same work, logging into Galileo, checking DynamoDB, opening Mixpanel, searching Zendesk, takes 15-30 minutes per card.

Results

The following table tracks Greenlight’s security operations on the metrics that matter most to the SOC. It compares three stages: manual triage before Luna, Tier 1 automation, and the full Tier 1 and Tier 2 system.

MetricBefore LunaWith Tier 1With Tier 1 and Tier 2
Autonomous resolution rate0% (all manual)83%More than 90%
Cases processed per month3,000-4,0003,000-4,0003,000-4,000
Median time-to-triage (routine)15-30 minutesSecondsSeconds
Human analyst escalations100% of cases17%<10%
Cost avoidanceBaselineSignificantEquivalent of multiple full-time employees
Risk reductionBaselineFaster detectionConsistent 24/7 quality

Estimated analyst time avoided:

Based on Greenlight’s case volume and manual handling-time measurements, processing 4,000 cases at 15–30 minutes each would require approximately 1,000–2,000 analyst hours per month. Greenlight reports that Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of these cases, avoiding an estimated 900–1,800 hours of routine manual work each month. Analysts can focus instead on cases that require human judgment.

The risk reduction comes from two factors: speed (seconds compared to minutes reduces the exposure window) and consistency (Luna applies the same triage logic at 3 AM on Saturday that it does at 10 AM on Tuesday, with no fatigue and no shortcuts).

Five lessons from building Luna

Building Luna and expanding it from security operations into financial risk surfaced five lessons for teams building multi-agent systems in regulated environments:

1. Start with a bounded domain, then expand horizontally

Greenlight started with security triage because the success criteria were clear: resolve the case correctly or escalate. After the pattern proved reliable at 83 percent resolution, expanding financial risk required adding new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor, not rebuilding the architecture.

2. Mirror your human team structure

The Tier 1/Tier 2 pattern maps directly to how SOC teams already operate. L1 analysts handle volume with playbooks. L2 analysts handle the complex cases with investigation skills. This made trust-building with the security team faster. They understood the model intuitively because it matched their own escalation logic.

3. Memory compounds in value

The episodic and long-term memory layer is what moved Luna from 83 percent to more than 90 percent. Each resolved case teaches Luna something: a new allowlisted pattern, a confirmed false positive source, a resolution template. After 6 months of operation, Luna has accumulated institutional knowledge that would take a new human analyst months to build.

4. Triage first, action later

In a regulated environment, Greenlight designed Luna to triage and recommend, not to take autonomous remediation actions without explicit policy approval. The risk expansion follows the same principle. Luna provides evidence supporting its recommendation. In this human-in-the-loop model, a human analyst or an approved automated policy authorizes and executes remediation. This separation satisfied Greenlight’s compliance requirements and built trust with the risk team.

5. Share specialized agents across domains

When Greenlight expanded into financial risk, they reused existing specialized agents (Datadog, Zendesk, Mixpanel) and added domain-specific ones (Galileo, fraud scoring). The same agent that checks Zendesk tickets for security cases also checks them for risk cases. This reduces maintenance overhead and helps keep consistency across domains.

Infrastructure stack

Luna runs entirely on managed AWS services. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the orchestration runtime, and the rest of the stack handles scheduling, messaging, state, secrets, and integration. The following table lists each service and its role in the infrastructure:

ServiceRole
Amazon Bedrock AgentCoreMulti-agent orchestration runtime. VPC deployment, private subnets, direct code through ZIP and S3
Amazon EventBridgeScheduled rate-based triggers for Tier 2 deep-dive triage cycles
Amazon SNSQueue completions and notification routing between tiers
Amazon DynamoDBLearnings storage, case deduplication, resolution pattern persistence
Amazon S3Agent packages and Terraform state management
Amazon CloudWatch Logs30-day retention for audit trails and compliance evidence
AWS Secrets ManagerExternal API credentials
AWS LambdaIngestion, resolution post-processing, kickoff, and digest functions
Amazon API GatewayLuna Queue API and MCP endpoint for external integrations

What Greenlight is building next

Building on the security and risk foundation, Greenlight is extending Luna’s multi-agent pattern into new operational domains and tooling:

  • Full risk domain coverage – Autonomous triage for financial and business risk cases (in progress, launched about one month ago).
  • Product operations – Exploring AWS DevOps Agent for incident investigation, root-cause analysis, and mitigation guidance. Greenlight is also evaluating how Luna’s existing agents could support operational investigations where their capabilities overlap.
  • Custom operational workflows – Exploring AWS DevOps Agent custom agents, skills, and Model Context Protocol integrations for repeatable operational workflows and access to Greenlight’s internal tools.
  • AWS DevOps Agent and skills – Combining the UI and skills framework of AWS DevOps Agent for script execution workflows (90-second execution time limit).
  • Well-Architected reviews – Exploring Model Context Protocol servers for automated infrastructure assessments against AWS best practices.

Conclusion

According to Greenlight’s production measurements, Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of the company’s security and risk cases and processes up to 4,000 cases each month. Cases requiring additional judgment are escalated to human analysts. This human-in-the-loop approach allows Greenlight to automate routine triage while retaining control over remediation decisions.

Teams in other regulated industries can apply the same approach by starting with a bounded use case, defining clear escalation criteria, and adding specialized agents and memory as the system matures. After the initial pattern proves reliable, teams can extend it to related operational domains.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

About the authors

item.title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bed…
item.description: Full title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard.

But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics.

In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist, the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic.

What the assistant had to get right

A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built:

  • Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so.
  • Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open.
  • No tax advice – Explaining how Taxbit computes cost basis (the accounting method used to compute a gain or loss) is product documentation. Telling a user which method to elect is tax advice. The line between the two is narrow.
  • Regional data residency – Supported from a single codebase, with continuous quality measurement in production.
  • Inside our compliance program – Taxbit Assist is developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Taxbit is also certified to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27701 and holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Taxbit doesn’t train or fine-tune any model, and Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or completions to train models.

We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows.

Solution overview

Taxbit Assist is a Strands Agents SDK application running on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram illustrates the solution architecture.

Figure 1: Request flow from a dashboard question through guardrails screening, knowledge base retrieval, model reasoning, permission checks, and response streaming

The workflow consists of the following steps:

  • A user asks a question in the Taxbit dashboard. A streaming chat API forwards it to AgentCore runtime along with the user’s verified identity (email, organization ID, and dashboard roles).
  • The runtime screens the incoming message with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Personally identifiable information (PII) is masked in place. If the message is blocked, the model is never invoked.
  • The agent retrieves candidate passages from an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases knowledge base, and then reranks them server-side. The knowledge base uses the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability of Amazon Bedrock, backed by Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • Amazon Bedrock models reason over the retrieved passages and verify that the user has access to the relevant feature and role before recommending any workflow. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region.
  • The answer streams back to the dashboard with source links. AgentCore memory carries the conversation across turns.
  • Every request emits OpenTelemetry traces to Amazon CloudWatch, which feeds our evaluation tooling.

The agent runtime

The agent is a small Python application: a system prompt, a model, and eight tools. It ships as an ARM64 container image that AgentCore runtime pulls from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and scales on demand.

The tools are deliberately narrow:

  • Knowledge base search, the primary tool.
  • Two access checks, one for organization entitlement and one for the user’s dashboard role.
  • Four support ticket tools to create, list, update, and close the caller’s own tickets.
  • Current time, for the rare question that needs sub-day precision.

In this version, the agent has no read access to customer tax data. It answers from product knowledge, and the only writes it can perform are the caller’s own support tickets.

One security decision underpins all of them: the model never handles identity. The user’s email, organization ID, and roles come from the trusted calling service and are bound into each tool through a closure before the model sees it. The model can decide whether to check permissions but not whose permissions to check, because identity isn’t a parameter it can set. User input is sanitized at the boundary, so a prompt injection cannot imitate the trusted context line.

The agent runs a foundation model (FM) through Amazon Bedrock, invoked through cross-Region inference profiles.

Geography-aware inference handles data residency. The inference profile ID carries a geography prefix derived from the deployment Region, so EU deployments keep inference within the EU, and US deployments stay in the US. Beyond keeping inference in the right geography, we also support a bring your own key (BYOK) model. In BYOK accounts, conversation history and the other stores that hold client data are encrypted with the customer’s own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key.

Application inference profiles handle cost visibility. Each deployment wraps the system inference profile in a tagged application profile, so every model invocation carries cost-allocation tags and shows up in AWS Cost Explorer, broken down by workload.

Amazon Bedrock prompt caching cuts latency and token cost. The system prompt is byte-identical for every request and ends with a cache checkpoint, so the static prefix is cached across users. Per-request context travels on the user message instead.

Grounding answers in a curated knowledge base

Most of our engineering effort went into the knowledge base: an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Amazon S3 Vectors, with Cohere Embed English v3 for embeddings, producing 1,024-dimension float32 vectors compared by cosine distance. All of it is managed, so there is no vector database for us to operate.

Ingestion

Content flows in from three kinds of sources, each landing under its own prefix in a single Amazon S3 bucket.

The following diagram shows how content reaches the index.

Figure 2: Content ingestion pipeline from published, code-derived, and curated sources through Lambda scrapers into Amazon S3 and the knowledge base

Published content comes first: our public website, our API documentation, and our help-center articles, crawled by scheduled AWS Lambda functions. With sitemap lastmod timestamps and content hashes, a typical run only touches what changed since the previous one. Scoping mattered more than we anticipated. Our sitemap has roughly over 400 URLs, but only about over 70 belong in an answer-generating corpus, and /blogs/ alone accounts for more than 300 marketing pages.
