For a noul question, the probability of true becomes the value and the most probable answer becomes the label. For a score question, the value is the probability-weighted expected level scaled to [0, 1]. For a choice question, it is the weighted average of predefined option values.

Validate a decision-model evaluator on your own traffic

When you rewrite a rubric as a decision model question, you’ve created a new measurement rather than a copy of the old one. A reframed rubric often lands stricter or looser than the original intended, and you won’t see that drift until you check it against real sessions. Before you gate a release on a decision-model evaluator, validate it the same way you’d validate any new measurement, against a labeled sample of your own traffic. The goal of this section is to walk you through that validation end to end, so you finish with an evaluator you can threshold with confidence.

The procedure has five steps.

Step 1. Build a labeled sample. Pull a set of stored sessions from your agent’s traffic, with enough coverage of the failures and edge cases you care about. A sample that covers only the happy path tells you nothing about where the evaluator breaks.

Step 2. Get human reference labels. Have three independent labelers score each turn for the property your question measures and take the majority vote as the reference label. Keep track of which turns were unanimous and which were split. Although unanimous turns are the clear-cut cases, the split-vote turns are the valuable ones, because they reveal ambiguity in the rubric itself before the model ever sees it.

Step 3. Run both evaluators on the same inputs. Run the decision-model evaluator and the matching built-in evaluator over those same sessions in a single batch evaluation. Scoring identical inputs is what makes the comparison apples to apples.

Step 4. Read the results through three lenses. With the majority-vote labels and the easy and hard split in hand, you can now answer the three questions that tell you whether the evaluator is ready.

  • Agreement rate: does it match your humans? Measure how often each evaluator agrees with the majority-vote labels, and do it per question, since one question’s accuracy says nothing about another’s. Then break the numbers out by easy (unanimous) and hard (split-vote) cases. An evaluator that stumbles only on the hard cases is behaving a lot like your human labelers did, which is exactly what you want.
  • Calibration: do the confidence scores mean something? Group turns by the evaluator’s reported probability and compare each group’s agreement with the labels. Higher confidence should track higher accuracy. Then check whether easy cases consistently draw higher confidence than hard ones. If they do, the model’s uncertainty is tracking genuine ambiguity, and you can use those groups to pick a decision threshold per evaluator instead of defaulting to 0.5.
  • Disagreement analysis: where and why do they differ? Find the turns where the two evaluators disagree with each other, and check whether those are the same turns your humans found ambiguous. Read them. Most disagreements trace back to the wording of the question, and a revised question clears them up. When the errors cluster in the hard cases, the rubric is the problem rather than the model.

Step 5. Re-run the check when anything changes. Treat this as a repeatable check rather than a one-time gate. Any time you reword a question or move to a new model version, run it again. Each result’s explanation records the model version that produced it, so you know which version a given score came from.

Choosing the best set of evaluators for your agent

The built-in evaluators remain the foundation of broad evaluation strategy in AgentCore Evaluations. They assess the response against a rubric and its supporting context, and explain the judgment so developers can investigate what went wrong. For the HR Assistant, a faithfulness evaluation can identify a claim that contradicts a tool result, whereas a helpfulness evaluation can point out that the agent answered a balance question but left a requested action incomplete.

Faithfulness, helpfulness, and correctness can require connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a solution. The preprint JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure describes a related distinction as “reading versus deriving.” A narrow decision-model check can flag a turn for attention, whereas the built-in evaluator provides the broader assessment and reasoning needed to review it. Decision models shine brightest when you treat them as a gate rather than a replacement. The cascade pattern works like this. First, run a fast, calibrated decision model on every turn of every session to get a cheap pass/fail signal. Then invoke a full LLM evaluator only on sessions where the signal falls below your threshold.

Figure 4: The cascade pattern, where a calibrated decision model screens every turn and only low-confidence turns escalate to a built-in evaluator

CriterionLLM as JudgeDecision Models as Judge
OutputScore + explanationCalibrated probability
Latency2–10 s~hundreds of ms (network)
CustomizableLimited (fixed prompt templates)Question definitions
Best forQualitative nuance, explanationCalibrated judgment

We recommend the following setup:

  • Configure online evaluation with the built-in evaluators you rely on, as the standard measure of quality across your agents.
  • Add decision-model evaluators for domain-specific yes/no and choice questions to the same configuration, along with deterministic code-based evaluators for anything you can compute exactly.
  • Each week, or on whatever schedule suits your release cycle, query the online results for sessions where a decision-model check failed or scored near its threshold, and run batch evaluations on those sessions with the built-in evaluators to get explanations.
  • Gate releases on the built-in evaluators and on the decision-model evaluators you have validated against labeled data, and track how often the two agree.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, run the cleanup.py that deletes the agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, the evaluators and evaluation config, the AWS Lambda functions that are registered as the evaluators, the EC2 instance that hosts the Strands Decider model, AWS Secrets Manager key and the associated log group on CloudWatch.

Conclusion

In this post, you connected two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to AgentCore Evaluations using code-based evaluators, and the accompanying code sample gives you a framework for testing those models and seeing where they add value as evaluators. The built-in evaluators remain your baseline. Decision models add narrow, validated checks that come with a measure of certainty you can threshold and act on. The practical path forward is to add decision-model checks alongside the built-in evaluators you already run, measure how often they agree with your reference labels on your own traffic, and expand coverage only once you trust them.

To get started, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations documentation, integrate custom evaluators using code-based evaluators and take a deeper look into Strands Decider model. Get started with code samples by deploying the sample evaluators from the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore sample repository.

About the authors

item.title: Smart Approvals in AWS Quick: Human oversight where it matte…
item.description: Full title: Smart Approvals in AWS Quick: Human oversight where it matters
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters

How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts, even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review.

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work.

Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked

Policy sets the boundary

Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions.

Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them.

How eligible actions are reviewed

Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service.

An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions.

The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct.

When an action goes beyond the request

An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context.

Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience.

Audit evidence and investigation

The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting.

Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations. Because chat logs can contain sensitive content, restrict access and consider CloudWatch Logs data protection policies to mask sensitive data.

Where to start

Because Smart Approvals is on by default, begin by confirming that actions requiring human approval are configured through connector action permissions. Set up a CloudTrail trail and delivery of chat logs and agent metadata logs to CloudWatch Logs to support investigations. Chat logs capture only activity after delivery is configured, so earlier approvals will lack that conversation context. With approval requirements and logging in place, use Custom Permissions to limit Smart Approvals to a pilot team working on a defined workflow before extending it to other teams.

Before the pilot, define what success looks like: fewer prompts for routine actions, with consequential actions still returning to a person for review. During the pilot, review a sample of automatic approvals and test high-impact cases, such as sending content outside the organization or adding a recipient introduced by a document. Confirm that these cases come back to the user. Confirm that your team can trace each action from approval through execution. Expand to more teams and workflows only when the results meet those criteria, and reassess as actions and policies change.

The measure of effective oversight isn’t how often an agent asks for approval, but whether people retain control over consequential decisions. For security leaders, the case for expanding Smart Approvals should rest on evidence from the pilot. Fewer prompts are valuable when they preserve attention without weakening accountability.

For setup steps, see Smart Approvals in the governance section of the Amazon Quick User Guide.

About the author

item.title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents:…
item.description: Full title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code

When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent.

This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout.

Post series

  • Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them.
  • Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code.
  • Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!)

The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK, Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations.

What is context engineering?

Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes.

Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing.

“As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).”
— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently.

How to handle tasks that exceed the context window

Anthropic has published several techniques for handling long-horizon tasks. Deep Insight groups these techniques into four layers, with each layer addressing the limitations of the others. The following table sets out the four layers.

LayerPracticeCore PrincipleLimitations
Layer 1: ArchitectureIsolating Context Through Multi-Agent ArchitectureEach agent operates in an independent contextWhen isolation alone is not enough
Layer 2: PromptOutput Control and Behavioral RulesLimiting context intake through promptsWhen prompts alone are not enough
Layer 3: ToolsFile-based Context ExternalizationKeeping heavy content in files outside the contextWhen issues still arise
Layer 4: Verification Agents and SafeguardsIndependent Verification and SafeguardsCatching errors and preventing context overflowFinal line of defense

The sections that follow take each layer in order, stating what the layer prescribes, why the preceding layers alone are insufficient, and how the practice is implemented in Deep Insight.

1. Isolating context through multi-agent architecture

Give each specialized agent its own context window and pass only compressed results to the orchestrator. Deep Insight does this with a hierarchy of Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, Supervisor, and Tool Agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker, Auditor).

With a single agent, all information, from user requests through data exploration, analysis, chart generation, validation, and reporting, accumulates in one context and easily exceeds the window. Giving each agent its own context keeps even the Coder, which uses the most, under 25K tokens total. Each agent receives only what it needs and signals others with a completion notice and brief summary.

The key to isolation is minimizing shared information. Deep Insight uses a Python dictionary, shared_state, that stores only four things:

  • messages: The previous agent’s final message (not the full conversation history).
  • clues: Compressed summaries collected from each agent.
  • full_plan: A checklist generated by Planner and updated by Tracker.
  • history: A brief log of agent names and messages.

The clues use a fixed CLUES_FORMAT: instead of each agent’s full conversation (tens of thousands of tokens), only compressed core results are passed.

# coder_agent_tool.py -- context passing format
CLUES_FORMAT = "Here is clues from {}:\n\n<clues>\n{}\n</clues>\n\n"
RESPONSE_FORMAT = "Response from {}:\n\n<response>\n{}\n</response>\n\n*Please execute the next step.*"

# After Coder completes: add only compressed result to clues
clues += CLUES_FORMAT.format("coder", response["text"])

This pattern is the one recommended in Anthropic’s “How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System” post, which describes an orchestrator-worker pattern in which a lead agent delegates to specialized subagents, with each agent working only within its own context. You do not need to build it yourself: the agents-as-tools pattern in the Strands Agents SDK provides this isolation at the framework level.

2. Controlling context inflow through prompts

Layer 1 isolation alone is not sufficient: even with independent contexts, an agent that generates long responses inflates the Supervisor’s context. Layer 2 limits each agent’s output through prompts.

For Deep Insight, we use prompts to limit how much information each agent returns to the Supervisor. Three rules do most of the work, as Deep Insight’s prompts show.

“Start with the strongest model and a simple prompt. Then incrementally add specific instructions based on actually observed failure cases.”
— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Implementation detail 2-1: Explicit per-agent output token budgets

Each agent’s prompt specifies a maximum response token count, preventing long responses that pollute the Supervisor’s context.

AgentOutput Token BudgetReason
Coder1,000–1,500 tokensAnalysis code is saved to files, so the agent returns only a summary of state, completed tasks, and insights
Validator800 tokensValidation results are saved to citations.json. The agent returns only a summary
Reporter1,000 tokensThe agent generates the report as a DOCX file and returns only a summary of the result

Anthropic’s ” Writing Effective Tools for Agents” post suggests giving tools a CONCISE or DETAILED response option for context efficiency. Apply the same idea one level up, in each agent’s system prompt. In Deep Insight, all agents share one standardized format:

## Status
[SUCCESS | PARTIAL_SUCCESS | ERROR]
## Completed Tasks
- [Task 1 from FULL_PLAN -- use exact wording so Tracker can match]
- [Task 2 -- be specific, not generic]
## Key Insights
- [Key finding 1 with numbers and ratios]
- [Key finding 2 with business implications]
## Generated Files
- ./artifacts/chart.png -- brief description
- ./artifacts/calculation_metadata.json -- N calculations

Implementation detail 2-2: Self-contained code philosophy

The Coder agent’s prompt explicitly states “variables do not persist between scripts.” Every script must include all necessary imports and load data directly. The prompt provides both incorrect and correct examples:

# WRONG -- Attempting to use a variable from Turn 1 in Turn 2
# Turn 1:
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
total = df['Amount'].sum()

# Turn 2:
print(f"Total: {total}")  # NameError: name 'total' is not defined

# CORRECT -- Every script is self-contained
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('./artifacts/cache/df_main.csv')  # Load from cache
total = df['Amount'].sum()
print(f"Total: {total}")

The reason this rule relates to context engineering is that referencing variables from previous scripts requires the agent to “remember” prior conversations, which means past code must remain in context. The self-contained principle means past code can be safely removed from context.

Implementation detail 2-3: Supervisor’s section completion rule

The Supervisor’s prompt includes the rule “Do not move to the next agent until all checklist items in the current agent’s section are marked [x].” We express this rule in the prompt because deciding whether the Coder’s work is complete requires the Supervisor to interpret the plan using information from the Tracker’s updates. This judgment is difficult to express in code alone.

3. “Only pointers in context, actual data in files”

Layer 1 isolates context between agents, and Layer 2 limits output within agents. But when the Coder agent generates 100 lines of Python code, that code itself enters the context. Even with “respond briefly” prompt instructions, some code can’t be written briefly. Layer 3 uses tool design to move heavy content outside the context, into the filesystem. Four techniques carry most of the benefit, as the following implementation details show.

Implementation detail 3-1: Moving code outside context with Write and Execute Tool

The Coder reads the analysis plan, writes Python, and executes it to generate visualizations. But when the code gets long, the conventional approach (separate file-write and execute tools) adds 100 lines directly to context per script, accumulating over 1,000 lines.

The fix is to collapse the two steps into a single tool, so the code never enters context as a message. Deep Insight’s Coder agent uses one write_and_execute_tool for this.

Here’s part of the write_and_execute_tool. After writing and executing the file, it returns only a summary: “Wrote 105 lines, execution successful, completed analysis of five categories.” The code stays in the file and about three lines of summary remain in context. Based on this example, that saves about 95 percent of the tokens.

# write_and_execute_tool.py
def _handle_write_and_execute_tool(file_path, content, timeout=300):
    """Write a Python script and immediately execute it."""
    # Step 1: Write file
    with open(file_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(content)
    # Step 2: Execute immediately
    result = subprocess.run(
        f"python {file_path}",
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        timeout=timeout
    )
    # Return only summary
    return f"Written {len(content.split(chr(10)))} lines to {file_path}\n" \
        f"Execution successful\n" \
        f"Output: {result.stdout[:500]}"  # Only first 500 chars
“Server-side filtering: filtering data at the execution layer before it reaches context, 98.7% token reduction (150K to 2K).”
— Anthropic, “Code Execution with MCP” (2025.11)

Implementation detail 3-2: Reusing common logic as modules in the Coder agent

Common modules get reused across analyses. Rather than regenerating them each time, define frequently-used functions as a module once and import them, which prevents token waste and context duplication.

Without this, defining functions like to_python_type() or track_calculation() in every analysis produces 200–300 lines of duplicate code across 10 analyses. Deep Insight generates a module called coder_analysis_utils.py before the first task. It includes functions for converting numpy types, tracking calculation metadata, and saving to JSON. Subsequent analyses import it, replacing 20–30 regenerated lines with two import lines, which saves tokens and improves consistency and debugging.

# coder_analysis_utils.py -- common module generated before first task
import numpy as np
import json
from datetime import datetime

_calculations = []

def to_python_type(value):
    """Convert numpy/pandas types to Python native types"""
    if isinstance(value, (np.integer, np.int64)): return int(value)
    elif isinstance(value, (np.floating, np.float64)): return float(value)
    elif isinstance(value, np.ndarray): return value.tolist()
    return value

def track_calculation(calc_id, value, description, formula,
                      source_file, source_columns, importance):
    """Track calculation metadata -- Validator independently verifies later"""
    _calculations.append({
        "id": calc_id, "value": to_python_type(value),
        "description": description, "formula": formula,
        "source_file": source_file, "source_columns": source_columns,
        "importance": importance
    })

def save_calculation_metadata(path="./artifacts/calculation_metadata.json"):
    """Save all tracked calculations to JSON"""
    with open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        json.dump({"generated_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),
                   "calculations": _calculations}, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

Implementation detail 3-3: Saving and sharing analysis results through structured note-taking

We use structured note-taking to share detailed analysis results without passing them through each agent’s context. Deep Insight stores these results in a file called all_results.txt, which is then read by agents as needed.

For example, the Coder agent appends results to all_results.txt after each analysis task:

with open('./artifacts/all_results.txt', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write(f"""
## Category Sales Analysis (completed at: 14:32)
- Top revenue category: Fruit (417,166,008 KRW, 45% of total)
- Top 3 categories: Fruit, Vegetables, Meat (78% of total)
- Generated file: ./artifacts/category_sales_chart.png
""")

The Coder records detailed results in this file after each analysis, and the Reporter reads it when writing the final report. Other agents collaborate through all_results.txt the same way.

Without note-taking, the Coder passes detailed results to the Supervisor after every task, accumulating in its context. With note-taking, only an approximately 30-token message like “Category sales analysis complete, 3 key insights found, detailed results saved to all_results.txt” is passed, and the Reporter reads the file when needed.

The pattern generalizes beyond a single file. The filesystem itself can serve as the inter-agent communication bus, as it does in Deep Insight:

File nameProducerConsumerRole
all_results.txtCoderReporterCumulative log of analysis results
calculation_metadata.jsonCoderValidatorRecord of numeric calculations: sources, formulas, and values (for verification)
citations.jsonValidatorReporterVerified citation data (inserted as [1], [2] in the report)
audit_findings.jsonAuditorReporterCitation defects found in the final report (drives targeted Reporter retries)
coder_analysis_utils.pyCoderAll scriptsShared utility functions (write once, import repeatedly)
full_plan (shared_state)Planner/TrackerSupervisorChecklist status (updating [x])
“The”just in time” approach, dynamically loading data into context at runtime rather than pre-processing all relevant data up front, keeps context fresh, relevant, and adaptive to the evolving state of the task.”
— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Implementation detail 3-4: Loading only needed knowledge with Skills

Rather than putting all specialized knowledge into the system prompt, this approach loads it only when needed. Including every skill guide (data structure checking, README generation, skill creation, system prompt writing, tool creation) would add over 20K tokens, load unnecessary information into the Coder agent on every call, and force a redeploy to add a skill.

Deep Insight’s Skills system loads only a skill catalog of about 500 tokens at startup, with the skill list holding only names and brief descriptions. When a user requests “Create a README file,” the agent decides “I need the readme-generator skill” and calls skill_tool(skill_name="readme-generator"). The SkillLoader reads readme-generator/SKILL.md and returns a detailed guide of about 3K tokens.

# 1. Skill Discovery (at initialization)
from src.utils.skills.skill_utils import initialize_skills
available_skills, skill_prompt = initialize_skills(
    skill_dirs=["./skills"],
    verbose=True
)

# 2. Add to System Prompt (~500-token catalog)
system_prompt = base_prompt + skill_prompt

# 3. Runtime -- Agent loads skill when needed
# Agent decides: "This is README generation, I need the readme-generator skill"
# -> skill_tool(skill_name="readme-generator")
# -> Returns full SKILL.md content (~3K tokens)

Each skill is defined as a SKILL.md file composed of YAML frontmatter and detailed markdown guide. It includes metadata like name, description, license, and allowed-tools, along with Overview, When to Use This Skill, detailed instructions, and Best Practices. To add a new skill, create a new directory under skills/ and write a SKILL.md file, and it is automatically discovered.

At startup, the agent loads a skill catalog of about 500 tokens instead of wasting over 20,000 tokens on full guides (about 97 percent less). When needed, it can load an additional few thousand tokens’ worth of detailed instructions for skills.

4. Verifying quality with verification agents and safeguards

Even with Layers 1–3, one risk remains: isolated agents can’t see each other’s work, so if the Coder miscalculates, the Reporter carries that error into the report. Layer 4 is the final line of defense.

“Provide testing tools so the agent can self-verify features and fix bugs that aren’t obvious from the code alone. Have the model commit its progress to git with descriptive commit messages and write progress summaries in a progress file.”
— Anthropic, “Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents” (2025.11)

Implementation detail 4-1: Tracker, Validator, and Auditor agents: progress tracking and quality assurance

Tracker updates the plan’s checklist in real time. When the Coder completes data loading, the Supervisor calls Tracker, which updates the plan item from [ ] to [x] based on information like “Data load complete (1,000 rows, 5 columns).” This helps both users and the system know exactly where progress stands.

Validator independently re-executes the Coder’s calculations to verify accuracy. It reads calculation_metadata.json, re-performs each calculation from source data, and compares: matches within 0.01 pass, mismatches are flagged. Verified calculations go to citations.json for the Reporter to cite. After the Reporter finishes, the Auditor checks the final DOCX against citations.json and calculation_metadata.json without modifying them. It records citation defects in audit_findings.json and can request up to two targeted retries from the Reporter.

Implementation detail 4-2: Prioritizing calculations for verification

Verifying every calculation is inefficient, so scope the verification by importance. Deep Insight’s OptimizedValidator applies the following thresholds:

  • Over 50 calculations: aggressive filtering, verify all high plus only 10 medium.
  • Over 20 calculations: moderate filtering, verify all high plus 15 medium.
  • 20 or fewer calculations: verify most, all high plus all medium plus 5 low.

It also applies type-safe comparison: to avoid numpy-versus-Python type issues, all values are converted to float() and checked for an absolute difference under 0.01:

# validator.md -- type-safe numerical comparison
try:
    match = abs(float(expected) - float(actual)) < 0.01
except:
    match = str(expected) == str(actual)

Implementation detail 4-3: SummarizingConversationManager: the last safety net

Context can still overflow in exceptional cases, so keep a safety net under the other layers. Deep Insight uses the SummarizingConversationManager in the Strands Agents SDK for this.

# strands_sdk_utils.py -- safety net configuration at agent creation
agent = Agent(
    model=llm,
    system_prompt=system_prompts,
    tools=tools,
    conversation_manager=SummarizingConversationManager(
        summary_ratio=0.5,  # summarize oldest 50% on overflow
        preserve_recent_messages=10,  # always preserve 10 most recent messages
        summarization_system_prompt=apply_prompt_template("summarization", {})
    )
)

On overflow, the LLM summarizes the oldest 50 percent of messages into one, while always preserving the 10 most recent to keep the current task’s context. The summarization prompt (summarization.md) requires clues, plans, and tracking status to be preserved verbatim.

Implementation detail 4-4: Selective prompt caching for cost optimization

Context engineering covers cost optimization, not only token savings. Enable prompt caching per agent, based on how often each is called with the same prompt. Deep Insight’s per-agent settings:

AgentPrompt CacheTool CacheReason
SupervisorYesYesHigh frequency of repeated calls, with a large system prompt and tool definitions
CoderYesYesRunning multiple analysis scripts sequentially, with the same prompt each time
ReporterYesYesGenerating a report incrementally section by section, with high prompt-reuse frequency
AuditorYesYesInspects the DOCX and JSON files over many turns with the same prompt and tools, and reruns after each Reporter retry
CoordinatorNoNoA single one-off call, no caching benefit
PlannerNoNoCalled once per request, and again only when the user requests a plan revision
ValidatorNoNoCalled with different data each time, low cache hit rate
TrackerNoNoLightweight task, no tools, caching unnecessary

Agents with caching enabled insert cache points into system prompts and tool definitions, reducing input token costs by up to 90 percent on repeated calls. This is a feature natively supported by the Strands Agents SDK. Plan Reviewer does not appear in the table because it’s a human-in-the-loop step that collects user approval or feedback rather than calling a model.

Conclusion

This post has detailed the four-layer engineering approach you can use to efficiently manage context for complex tasks that exceed the context window.

  • Layer 1 (architecture-level isolation): Each agent works in an independent context through multi-agent architecture, passing only compressed summaries.
  • Layer 2 (prompt-based control): Output token budgets, standardized response formats, and self-contained code philosophy actively limit context inflow.
  • Layer 3 (filesystem use): write_and_execute_tool keeps code outside context, the filesystem serves as an inter-agent communication bus, and knowledge is lazy-loaded only when needed.
  • Layer 4 (verification and safeguards): Validator’s independent calculation re-verification, Auditor’s read-only citation audit of the final report, Tracker’s progress tracking, SummarizingConversationManager’s overflow prevention, and selective prompt caching manage both quality and cost.

Each layer forms a defense system that compensates for what the preceding layers miss. When architecture isolation is insufficient, prompts limit output. When prompts are insufficient, tools keep content external. And when problems still arise, verification catches them.

Each of these layers is documented in Anthropic’s engineering posts, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents”, “Code Execution with MCP”, and “How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System”. Much of what they recommend already ships in the Strands Agents SDK rather than being something you build: SummarizingConversationManager, prompt caching, and the agents-as-tools pattern.

When building production agents, the LLM’s context window alone is rarely enough. Apply these context engineering techniques to manage context efficiently and scale your agents for production workloads.

Deep Insight, the reference implementation used here, is open source. Review the code and extend it for your domain.

  • GitHub
  • Workshop

About the authors

item.title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data qual…
item.description: Full title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences

This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited.

Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise.

This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs.

About Indegene

Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments.

Why conventional data quality programs break down

Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve.

One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult.

Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent.

Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly.

Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context.

As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability.

Rethinking data quality with generative AI

Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together.

Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP), a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication.

By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations:

  • Consolidate fragmented enterprise data into a trusted source of truth.
  • Standardize data quality and governance across business domains.
  • Improve metadata visibility, lineage, and traceability.
  • Reduce manual effort across data engineering workflows.
  • Deliver trusted, AI-ready data for enterprise analytics and decision-making.

Figure 1: NEXT Unified Data Platform dashboard with use cases and AI agents

Figure 2: NEXT UDP technical architecture on AWS

Indegene’s life sciences clients needed an agent that could run reliably in production and meet strict governance requirements, while giving the team flexibility in how they build it. Within NEXT UDP, Generative AI powers an intelligent Data Quality Agent that augments existing data quality processes. The agent boosts data engineer and data steward productivity by accelerating rule creation, simplifying validation, and helping maintain consistent governance at enterprise scale.

Indegene built the Data Quality Agent on a set of AWS services, with Amazon Bedrock, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at its core. Amazon Bedrock, provides a choice of foundation models (FMs), built on a foundation of security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. For life sciences organizations, this matters because their data often includes sensitive healthcare professional and patient information. Strands Agents streamlines building and updating the agent, and its evaluation tools help Indegene test rule accuracy, which is critical in regulated life sciences environments. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The solution also inherits existing AWS security and audit controls, so Indegene can focus on data quality logic instead of agent infrastructure.

What makes the Data Quality Agent unique? Two knowledge bases that power context-aware data quality

Any data quality tool can check for null values, duplicates, or invalid data types. Services such as AWS Glue Data Quality, a capability of AWS Glue, already recommend rules like these from data statistics, and they remain a strong foundation. The harder problem is determining whether the data makes sense for its business purpose. To address this, the Data Quality Agent uses two complementary knowledge bases that combine curated domain knowledge with experience gained from governed usage.

The first is an Internal Enterprise knowledge base: It combines internal business glossaries, data dictionaries, SOPs, regulatory guidance, approved data quality rules, validated scripts, profiling results, historical anomalies, and subject matter expert (SME) feedback. Content is ingested, vectorized, and retrieved through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate data quality rules grounded in enterprise standards and proven outcomes.

The second is an External Reference knowledge base: It’s built and periodically updated using approved standardized data quality frameworks, web search, and controlled web-scraping. When a dataset is selected, the agent analyzes table and column metadata and retrieves relevant data quality standards, reference values, and validation best practices from trusted sources. For example, for an NPI (National Provider Identifier) column, it can identify applicable quality standards, recommend format (the required 10-digit numeric format) and perform reference-validation checks.

How it works

Figure 3: Data Quality Agent process flow

The Data Quality Agent takes users from data profiling to rule creation and governance in a single workflow:

  • Select source: Connect to a supported source such as Amazon Redshift or Snowflake.
  • Select database and schema: Browse the available tables, with the rule count and active rule status for each.
  • Profile data: The solution computes quality metrics and column patterns for the table, which users review.
  • Detect anomalies: The solution flags anomalies against historical baselines, and users review the total, critical, and warning issues and the affected records.
  • Manage rules: Review a table’s existing rules or start creating new ones.
  • Choose rule mode: Pick Column Level, Table Level, or Custom Query.
  • Generate rule suggestions: The agent uses metadata, profiling results, anomalies, existing rules, and knowledge base context to recommend technical and business rules, each with a severity.
  • Review, refine and apply: Users edit or approve each recommendation.
  • Generate and validate code: The agent produces SQL and Python for approved rules, and a validation step checks them.
  • Store in the central rule repository: Approved rules become available for execution, monitoring, and audit.

Solution architecture of the generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent on AWS

The following diagram shows the end-to-end architecture of the Data Quality Agent on the NEXT UDP platform, from the data steward request to rule execution.

Figure 4: Solution architecture of the Data Quality Agent on NEXT UDP

Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution from the Indegene application. The following table provides a walkthrough of the solution pipeline and lists the AWS services used for each layer. It also captures other options the solution supports, so you can adapt it to your data volumes, existing tools, and operational preferences.

LayerAWS / platform servicesAlso supportedRole
API and accessAWS WAF, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Cognito–Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution through Amazon API Gateway. AWS WAF filters requests before they reach the API, and Amazon Cognito authenticates users with OAuth 2.0 and validates the JWT on each request.
Data source layerAmazon RedshiftSnowflake connector, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), JDBC/ODBC sourcesProvides structured and semi-structured data for data quality profiling and rule execution.
Metadata catalog layerAWS Glue Data CatalogAWS Glue crawlers for automatic schema discoveryCaptures databases, schemas, tables, columns, data types, and rule coverage.
Profiling and anomaly detection layerAWS Lambda (Python), with results stored in Amazon DynamoDBAWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQLColumn statistics, such as null rates, distinct counts, data type conformance, patterns, value ranges and table-level signals are computed by a Python-based profiling process on AWS Lambda, The same Lambda performs anomaly detection using statistical comparison against historical baselines to flag unexpected shifts, such as a null-rate spike or a cardinality change.
Knowledge/RAG layerAmazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector) and S3 for storing knowledge documents exposed as tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCoreAmazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector store, Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3Retrieves from the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (external reference standards and internal enterprise knowledge). AgentCore Gateway connects the agent to its knowledge bases as tools.
LLM intelligence layerStrands Agents on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, AgentCore memoryOther foundation models available in Amazon BedrockGenerates data quality rules and uses the assembled context and few-shot prompting to recommend both technical checks (completeness, format, uniqueness) and pharma-specific business rules. Amazon Bedrock provides a choice of FMs to generate rules. AgentCore runtime provides a managed, session-isolated environment, AgentCore memory retains reviewer feedback to improve future recommendations.
Orchestration and human review layerAWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge–Coordinates profiling, LLM calls, rule generation, rule execution, status updates, and human review.
Rule metadata repositoryAmazon DynamoDBAmazon Aurora / Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)Stores rule ID, name, type, column, status, author, created date, severity, and version details.
Code generation, validation and storageAmazon Bedrock – Claude Sonnet 4.5 and AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with approved scripts store in Amazon S3–Generates Python / SQL code and checks before storage
Execution layerAWS LambdaAWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQLRuns data quality checks and writes violation counts and detailed anomalies.
Monitoring and dashboard layerAmazon CloudWatch, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or application UIAmazon Quick, Amazon OpenSearch DashboardsData quality dashboard displays the rules applied and their status, along with total anomalies, critical anomalies, checks run, and issue details.
Security and governanceAWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), AWS Secrets Manager, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints–Authentication, encryption, secrets, audit, and threat detection

How the Data Quality Agent builds context

Before recommending any validation rule, the Data Quality Agent assembles context from six distinct sources, each answering a different question about the data:

Context SourceWhat it providesQuestion it answers
Table/Column Metadata (Catalog)Schema, data types from the Data CatalogWhat is this data?
Data ProfileColumn-level statistics computed from the actual data, such as null rates, distinct counts, value ranges, frequent values and detected patternsWhat does the data look like right now?
Anomaly Detection ResultsUnexpected changes flagged by comparing the latest profile with historical baselines, such as a sudden rise in nulls, a change in distinct values, or out-of-range valuesWhat has changed or looks wrong?
Existing Active Data Quality RulesRules already applied at the table or column level, retrieved from the rule repositoryWhat rules already exist, so we don’t duplicate or conflict?
External Reference Knowledge BaseUniversal, publicly established data quality standards and validation best practices (for example, format and structural rules for identifiers like the National Provider Identifier)What are the industry standards for this field?
Internal Enterprise Knowledge BaseOrganization-specific data quality rule patterns, prior reviewer feedback, and curated business/technical rule librariesHow does this organization define quality?

Together, these sources let the agent reason like an experienced data steward. Grounding every recommendation in what the data is, what the standards require, how the enterprise defines quality, and what has already been implemented.

What the solution does

The Data Quality Agent generates several categories of checks and keeps data stewards in control of the results.

Anomaly checks generation

The solution generates anomaly checks that catch values which are technically valid but don’t match how a pharmaceutical market behaves. These include negative switch percentages, market shares that don’t add up to 100 percent within a market, inconsistent drug rankings (for example, a drug ranked first with a lower share than the drug ranked second), rating values outside the defined scale, and panel sizes that are too small or don’t match the number of respondents.

Context-aware rule generation with RAG

The Data Quality Agent generates rule recommendations in three modes:

Rule TypeDescription
Column LevelGenerates data quality rules for a specific, individual column selected by the user. The agent reads that column’s metadata and profiling signals to suggest checks such as data type validation, null and mandatory-field checks, length and range validation, pattern/format validation, and uniqueness.
Table LevelGenerates data quality rules for the table as a whole, driven by the table’s metadata and relationships across its columns. This covers record consistency, duplicate detection, cross-column validation, referential integrity checks, and table-wide business consistency.
Custom QueryGenerates SQL-based rules from natural language input. The user describes the business validation in plain English and the agent produces the corresponding SQL, which can then be refined conversationally or edited directly to support complex validations that fall outside standard column and table checks.

The Create New Quality Rule interface provides dedicated Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query modes.

The platform supports both technical validation and business-specific quality checks.

For technical rules, the agent generates checks that confirm the data is structurally sound. These include null checks for mandatory fields, data type validation, range validation for numeric and date values, pattern validation for formatted fields such as identifiers and codes, duplicate detection, and referential integrity checks between related tables.

For business rules, the agent generates life sciences checks that confirm the data is consistent with how the business operates. These include account affiliation consistency (for example, a healthcare provider linked to the correct organization), segmentation logic, eligibility criteria, and market share and product share validation (for example, shares within a territory not exceeding 100%).

Real use-case example

Consider an HCP Product Performance table with the columns HCP_ID, Specialty, Territory_ID, Product_ID, Prescription_Volume, Market_Share_Pct, Switch_Pct, Rating_Scale, and Reporting_Month. Using the table profile and the two Knowledge Bases, this is how the Data Quality Agent generates and performs the following checks:

  • Anomaly checks performed. Negative switch percentage. Market share total mismatch. Sudden increase or decrease in prescription volume. Inconsistent product rankings. Invalid rating-scale values.
  • Technical rules generated. HCP_ID must not be null or duplicated. Prescription_Volume must be numeric and non-negative. Market_Share_Pct and Switch_Pct must be between 0 and 100. Reporting_Month must follow the required date format. Territory_ID and Product_ID must match their reference tables.
  • Business rules generated. Market share across all products must total 100 percent for each territory and reporting month. The HCP’s product eligibility must align with their specialty. Only eligible HCPs can be included in the target segment.

AI-assisted severity recommendation

The solution recommends severity based on dataset context, rule type, and business impact. Severity categories help distinguish between:

  • Critical issues, such as invalid commercial metrics, incorrect identifiers, or business rule violations.
  • Basic validations, including schema conformance, null checks, and length validation.
  • Complex validations involving advanced SQL logic, multi-column rules, or domain-specific business checks.
  • Information: Validation conducted for awareness and transparency purposes only. No action is required unless concerns are identified.

SQL/Python code generation and ETL integration

After a rule is approved, the LLM generates the equivalent SQL, Python, and PySpark code. Before it’s stored, the code is validated automatically with syntax checks, a check against the target schema, and a test run on sample data where the language supports it. This means existing extract, transform, and load (ETL) and orchestration tools can run them as part of the current data pipelines.

AI-assisted validation

Using an LLM as a Validation Agent to review data quality (DQ) rules/scripts generated by another LLM for reducing hallucinations and improving governance. Further, Amazon Bedrock provides security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. Prompts and outputs aren’t used to train the models or shared with model providers. Amazon Bedrock is HIPAA eligible and in scope for compliance programs such as SOC, ISO and GDPR, which helps Indegene meet the requirements of its life sciences clients. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails adds configurable safeguards on model inputs and outputs. It detects and masks personally identifiable information (PII), blocks harmful content and prompt injection attacks, and uses contextual grounding checks to flag responses that aren’t supported by the retrieved knowledge.

Human oversight remains central

The Data Quality Agent is designed to augment existing data quality processes. Each generated rule receives a confidence score. Only high-confidence, low-risk rules are approved automatically, while critical and business rules always go to an SME for review. Every decision is recorded in the rule repository, so rule management stays governed, traceable, and aligned with enterprise standards.

Delivering operational impact and business value

In production, across Indegene’s deployments of NEXT UDP for life sciences clients, the Data Quality Agent has reduced the effort to define and implement data quality rules from about 30 hours to about 4 hours per dataset. That’s roughly 85 percent less effort, or about 7x higher productivity. Onboarding a new table now takes 2–4 hours instead of 2–5 working days. Data engineers and data stewards now spend their time reviewing and approving rules rather than writing them from scratch.

Key outcomes include:

  • Less manual effort through AI-generated rules, SQL, and Python.
  • Faster onboarding of new tables, schemas, and business domains.
  • More consistent rules, grounded in approved standards, enterprise knowledge, and existing rules.
  • Better collaboration between business and technical teams through the review, refine, and approve workflow.
  • Earlier detection of data quality issues through automated profiling and anomaly detection.

Table 1: Performance and Scale

MetricImpact*
Enterprise profiling25–50 schemas; 500–2,000 tables; 10,000–50,000 columns
Table profiling45–90 sec (~1M rows); 2–5 min (~10M rows)
AI rule generation20–45 sec per table
SQL generation3–8 sec per rule; 20–60 sec for 10–15 rules
Rule execution20–30 sec (standard); 1–3 min (complex SQL)
Central rule repository1,000–10,000 rules
DQ checks per execution100–500 per domain. Scalable to 1,000+

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 2: Rule quality and validation

MetricImpact*What does it mean
Rule suggestion accuracy80–90%Suggestions that are technically valid and apply correctly to the column or table
Rule acceptance rate60–75%Suggestions approved without any changes
Rule refinement rate / Human Override Rate20–35%Suggestions approved after the reviewer edited logic or thresholds
SQL validity90–97% (schema-grounded); 80–90% (custom SQL)Generated SQL that passes validation on the first attempt
Severity recommendation accuracy75–85%Recommended severity matching the reviewer’s final severity
Business relevance (SME rating)4.0–4.5 / 5SME rating of how useful the recommended rules are to the business
Hallucination rate<5–8%Suggestions that reference non-existent columns or incorrect business logic

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 3: Operational efficiency

MetricImpact*
Manual SQL rule authoring60–80% reduction in end-to-end effort, including review and refinement
New table onboarding2–5 working days → 2–4 hours
Rule reuse40–60% of new rules adapted from existing approved rules
LLM cost optimizationUp to 90% lower input-token cost on cached context with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
Compute optimization~45–51% reduction with metadata-first profiling

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 4: Manual compared to agent-assisted data quality

ActivityTraditional DQ ApproachGenerative AI-powered DQ approachImpact*
Rule DiscoveryManual review of schemas, profiling reports, sample data, and documentation. Existing tools can generate basic profiling checks but often miss domain-specific business logicAgent uses metadata, profiling results, table context, existing rule patterns, and optional business descriptions to recommend technical and life sciences-specific data quality rules80-85% faster
Technical Rule GenerationManual creation of null, data type, range, uniqueness, and integrity rulesAutomated rule generation with human review80-85% faster
Business Rule DefinitionValidation is often based on technical metadata with limited understanding of product, segment, customer, or eligibility logic. Business context depends heavily on SME discussions and manual translation into validation logicUses RAG to retrieve business glossaries, data dictionaries, existing rules, and historical anomaly patterns to generate context-aware recommendations.70-75% faster
Rules authoring and SQL/Python DevelopmentEngineers manually define validation rules and perform coding, debugging, and testing for each dataset or business requirement.Auto-generated rules at the Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query levels, and generate SQL/Python for the selected DQ checks. Users can review, refine, and apply the recommendations.80-85% faster to first working code
Rule ValidationRules are validated manually, involving multiple iterations of executing the queries and refiningAgent scores, refines, and optimizes rules automatically80-85% faster
Rule ReuseManual copy, modify, and reuseApproved rules and feedback added to the agent’s knowledge50% faster onboarding for new datasets in an existing domain
Anomaly DetectionManual analysis of profiling outputs and recordsAutomated anomaly detection with business-context explanations80-85% faster
Severity classificationRule severity and business impact are determined manually, which can lead to inconsistent prioritization.Recommends severity based on rule type, dataset context, and business impact.Consistent, context-based severity
Governance & TraceabilityRules are often distributed across tools, scripts, spreadsheets, or catalogs, making governance and traceability difficult. Approval and review workflows vary across teams.Central, versioned rule repository with ownership85% reduction in maintenance effort
Human EffortSMEs and engineers drive every stepSMEs focus on review and approval. The agent handles discovery and generationHigher productivity & scalability, ~7x productivity

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Looking ahead

As enterprise data ecosystems continue to grow, maintaining consistent and scalable data quality becomes increasingly difficult using manual rule creation and fragmented governance processes. Generative AI provides an opportunity to augment these workflows by accelerating rule generation, incorporating business context, and supporting governed decision-making.

The generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent within the NEXT Unified Data Platform demonstrates how large language models, RAG, and centralized rule governance can work together to simplify data quality management while keeping humans in control of review and approval. Future enhancements will continue to build on this foundation, including:

  • AI-assisted remediation recommendations to help users resolve failed data quality checks.
  • Root cause analysis to identify recurring anomaly patterns and support faster investigation of repeated data quality issues.

As these capabilities evolve, the focus remains the same: helping organizations improve data quality through AI-assisted automation while maintaining governance, transparency, and business oversight.

To learn more, refer to the following resources:

  • Indegene in the life sciences space
  • Generative AI in Healthcare & Life Sciences
  • AWS Skill Builder course: Building Generative AI Applications Using Amazon Bedrock
  • GitHub repo: Sample Healthcare and Life Sciences Agents on AWS

About the authors

item.description: Full title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity.

When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer.

Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories.

In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it.

The problem: Too many systems, too much friction

U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud.

Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration.

The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars.

  • Reach: agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time.
  • Depth: chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis.
  • Community: a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division.

The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform

AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios.

What agentic means in practice

The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example.

With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply.

With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account.

In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems.

Architecture: Six layers, one interface

AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching.

The following diagram shows how the layers fit together.

Figure 1: AiDaH’s layered architecture

As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers.

Layer 1: Staff interface

Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers.

Layer 2: Orchestration

The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails, then enters a cost-optimized routing tier. Roughly 70 percent of requests resolve through deterministic keyword matching with no model invocation, 20 percent are classified by a lightweight model, and only 10 percent require the full orchestrator. The cheapest path that can confidently handle the request is the one that runs.

Layer 3: Specialist agents

Eight experts spanning customer relationship management, customer problem management, number portability, order and SIM operations, infrastructure monitoring, big data analytics, cloud cost management, and finance operations. They communicate over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which lets them delegate subtasks and complete cross-system workflows no single agent could handle alone.

Layer 4: Gateways and backend APIs

AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes U Mobile’s backends to agents through a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Behind each gateway sit AWS Lambda functions and MCP servers that translate agent intent into calls against a specific system.

Layer 5: Data and knowledge

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, grounds agent responses in governed content, using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Content spans a shared enterprise knowledge base and a separate finance corpus. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, maintains conversational context across turns, and Amazon DynamoDB holds the six-tier role-based access control model and session metadata.

Layer 6: Operational systems

U Mobile’s on-premises and cloud operational systems are reached over AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, an IPsec-encrypted tunnel with no public internet exposure.

How a request flows through the layers

Tracing a single request makes the interaction between the layers concrete. Consider a support agent who types a port-in status question into the AiDaH channel in Microsoft Teams.

  • Interface: The Teams message reaches an AWS Lambda function, which forwards the request and the caller’s federated identity to the orchestrator.
